The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be a nonempty oriented smooth link with $r\ge1$ components, and let $X_L=S^3\setminus L$ be its open complement. For each component choose a smooth fibrewise norm on its normal plane bundle $\nu(K_i)$ and a tubular map $\Phi_i$ from an open neighborhood of the zero section, fixing the zero section, together with a radius $\epsilon_i>0$ whose closed disk subbundle lies in that neighborhood. Require the resulting closed tubes $N(K_i)=\Phi_i(D_{\epsilon_i}\nu(K_i))$ to be pairwise disjoint, and put $N(L)=\bigcup_{i=1}^rN(K_i)$ and $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(L)$, the resulting compact smooth $3$-manifold with boundary. The tube choices are part of the input. Choose a basepoint $b\in E_L\subset X_L$. Orient each normal disk so that the positive tangent to $K_i$ followed by its positive normal basis agrees with the fixed orientation of $S^3$. A **positive meridian** $\mu_i$ of $K_i$ is the oriented boundary of the radius-$\epsilon_i$ normal disk in one fibre of $\nu(K_i)$; the curve lies on $\partial E_L$ and is disjoint from every component of $L$; its spanning normal disk meets $K_i$ transversely once with positive sign and misses every other component. Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ and identifies the classes of $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r$ with its standard basis. Write $G=\pi_1(X_L,b)$ and let $\phi:G\to H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ be the first Hurewicz homomorphism, equivalently abelianization. The subgroup $\ker\phi$ is normal. The connected covering $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ classified by $\ker\phi$ is the **maximal abelian cover**; it is regular and its deck group is identified with $G/\ker\phi\cong H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$. Put $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)]\cong\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$, where $t_i$ is the deck transformation corresponding to $[\mu_i]$. The isomorphism sends each variable to its group-ring basis element; monomials $t_1^{n_1}\cdots t_r^{n_r}$ correspond bijectively to the basis elements indexed by $n_1[\mu_1]+\cdots+n_r[\mu_r]$. Define the absolute multivariable Alexander module by

$$A_L=H_1(X_L^{\mathrm{ab}};\mathbb Z),$$

as a left $\Lambda_r$-module under the deck action. “Absolute” means this is ordinary homology of the covering space, not relative homology with respect to a fibre over the basepoint.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Let $B$ be nonempty, path-connected, locally path-connected, and semilocally simply connected, fix $b_0\in B$, and put $G=\pi_1(B,b_0)$.

1. The assignment $$[p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)]\longmapsto p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$$ is a bijection from based-isomorphism classes of based connected coverings of $B$ to subgroups of $G$.
2. After forgetting the chosen point in the fibre, the assignment to the conjugacy class of $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$ is a bijection from isomorphism classes of connected coverings of $B$ to conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For every integer $r\ge1$, the commutative ring
$$
\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]
$$
is Noetherian and a unique factorisation domain. Its units are exactly the elements $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$ with $k_i\in\mathbb Z$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $L$ be a nonempty oriented $r$-component link with $r\ge1$ and maximal-abelian-cover module $A_L$ over $\Lambda_r=\mathbb Z[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Then $A_L$ is finitely presented, every elementary/Fitting ideal $E_j(A_L)$ is independent of the chosen finite triangulation and of the chosen lifts of its cells, and the order $\operatorname{ord}(A_L)$—the greatest common divisor of the generators of $E_q(A_L)$, where $q=\dim_{\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r)}(A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r}\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda_r))$—is defined up to a unit $\pm t_1^{k_1}\cdots t_r^{k_r}$. The diagonal ring map $\eta:\Lambda_r\to\Lambda_1=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$, $t_i\mapsto t$, specializes the lifted chain complex by coefficient extension to the total-linking cyclic-cover chain complex. This statement concerns the chain complex only; it does not identify $A_L\otimes_{\Lambda_r,\eta}\Lambda_1$ with the first homology of the specialized complex. For $r\ge2$, the diagonal map is nonflat and such an identification need not hold because homology need not commute with nonflat base change.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the data in the definition of the maximal-abelian-cover Alexander module for a nonempty oriented smooth link $L$. Let $i:E_L\hookrightarrow X_L$ be the inclusion of the compact exterior into the open complement, and let $p:X_L^{\mathrm{ab}}\to X_L$ be the maximal abelian cover. Then $E_L$ is a strong deformation retract of $X_L$, the restricted covering $p^{-1}(E_L)\to E_L$ is the connected maximal abelian cover of $E_L$, and the lifted deformation retract is equivariant under the deck group. The inclusion identifies $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$ with $H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)$ and preserves the positive-meridian classes. In particular, inclusion induces a $\Lambda_r$-module isomorphism

$$
H_1(p^{-1}(E_L);\mathbb Z)\cong A_L.
$$
Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, $H:Y\times I\to B$ a homotopy, and $\widetilde H_0:Y\to E$ a lift of $H(-,0)$. There is a unique lift $\widetilde H:Y\times I\to E$ of $H$ extending $\widetilde H_0$.

Let $A\subseteq X$, let $i:A\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and choose $a\in A$. If $A$ is a retract of $X$ ([[def-retraction-and-deformation-retract]]), then

$$i_*:\pi_1(A,a)\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,a)$$

is injective. If $A$ is a deformation retract of $X$, the inclusion and retraction induce mutually inverse fundamental-group isomorphisms at every basepoint of $A$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

derivations.claim: Every point of $S^3\setminus H$ has $z\ne0$ and $w\ne0$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto(z/|z|,w/|w|,|z|)$ has inverse $(u,v,s)\mapsto(su,\sqrt{1-s^2}v)$, so the open complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and a compact exterior is $T^2\times I$. The two phase loops are positive meridians of the two coordinate-circle components, hence form the basis of $\pi_1(E_H)=H_1(E_H;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$. By [F3], the maximal abelian cover is the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$, whose first homology vanishes. The compact-exterior/open-complement identification [F7] therefore gives $A_H=0$.

By [F1], the two positive meridians form the coordinate basis; the coordinate-sum definition [F2] therefore sends both to $1$, so its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(1,-1)$. Quotienting the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$ by this rank-one translation subgroup gives $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$. Its first homology is $\mathbb Z$ generated by the circle. Every deck transformation is represented by a translation, and the path of translations from the identity to that translation is a homotopy, so $t$ acts as $1$. Thus the cyclic module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)\ne0$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$ because $A_H=0$.

For the standard unknot $K=\{w=0\}$ in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, the exterior of the tube $|w|\le\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $D^2_{\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}}\times S^1$ by $(z,v)\mapsto(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\,v)$; hence it is a solid torus. For the split unlink use its given separating sphere, with one component and its tube in each ball. The exterior is a collared union along that sphere of two ball-minus-tube pieces. Each piece is a solid-torus unknot exterior with the interior of one disjoint standard ball removed. Reattaching the ball does not change fundamental group, by van Kampen with the simply connected sphere overlap. Thus each piece has group $\mathbb Z$ generated by its positive meridian. Van Kampen on their separating-sphere union gives $\pi_1(E_U)\cong\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z$ with these meridian generators. This does not identify $E_U$ with a handlebody or assert a graph deformation retraction.

Let $G=S^1\vee S^1$ map its two based oriented loops to these meridians in $E_U$. It induces the computed fundamental-group isomorphism and intertwines abelianization to $\mathbb Z^2$. Lift it to the connected maximal abelian covers after fixing the base lift. The induced map on fundamental groups identifies the kernels of abelianization, hence is an isomorphism. Degree-one Hurewicz then makes its map on first homology an isomorphism. This is Laurent-linear: conjugation by each meridian implements its deck action on the kernel abelianization, and the map intertwines those conjugations. The same argument for total linking to $\mathbb Z$ compares the cyclic-cover $H_1$. Only first homology is compared; the separating sphere is not removed by a false homotopy equivalence. The lifted graph cellular boundary is $C_1=\Lambda_2^2\xrightarrow{(t_1-1,\ t_2-1)}C_0=\Lambda_2$, so this graph complex computes the desired first homology.

The quotient $\Lambda_2/(t_1-1)$ is $\mathbb Z[t_2^{\pm1}]$, a domain by [F5], so $t_1-1$ is prime. It does not divide $t_2-1$, whose image under $t_1\mapsto1$ is the nonzero element $t_2-1$. If $(a,b)$ lies in the kernel, $(t_1-1)a=-(t_2-1)b$, so primality forces $t_1-1$ to divide $b$. Write $b=(t_1-1)c$; cancellation in the domain gives $a=-(t_2-1)c$. Thus the kernel is generated by $(-(t_2-1),t_1-1)$; it is free because its second coordinate can vanish only when $c=0$. Hence $A_U\cong\Lambda_2$.

Under total linking, both loop edges map to $t$, so [F6] gives the cyclic-cover boundary $(t-1,t-1):\Lambda_1^2\to\Lambda_1$. Since $\Lambda_1$ is a domain, its kernel consists of $(a,-a)$ and is free of rank one. This confirms the stated cyclic-cover module and completes the example.

derivations.claim: Every point of $S^3\setminus H$ has $z\ne0$ and $w\ne0$. The map $(z,w)\mapsto(z/|z|,w/|w|,|z|)$ has inverse $(u,v,s)\mapsto(su,\sqrt{1-s^2}v)$, so the open complement is $T^2\times(0,1)$ and a compact exterior is $T^2\times I$. The two phase loops are positive meridians of the two coordinate-circle components, hence form the basis of $\pi_1(E_H)=H_1(E_H;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^2$. By [F3], the maximal abelian cover is the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$, whose first homology vanishes. The compact-exterior/open-complement identification [F7] therefore gives $A_H=0$.

For the standard unknot $K=\{w=0\}$ in $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$, the exterior of the tube $|w|\le\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $D^2_{\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}}\times S^1$ by $(z,v)\mapsto(z,\sqrt{1-|z|^2}\,v)$; hence it is a solid torus. For the split unlink use its given separating sphere, with one component and its tube in each ball. The exterior is a collared union along that sphere of two ball-minus-tube pieces. Each piece is a solid-torus unknot exterior with the interior of one disjoint standard ball removed. Reattaching the ball does not change fundamental group, by van Kampen with the simply connected sphere overlap. Thus each piece has group $\mathbb Z$ generated by its positive meridian. Van Kampen on their separating-sphere union gives $\pi_1(E_U)\cong\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z$ with these meridian generators. This does not identify $E_U$ with a handlebody or assert a graph deformation retraction.

By [F1], the two positive meridians form the coordinate basis; the coordinate-sum definition [F2] therefore sends both to $1$, so its kernel in $\mathbb Z^2$ is generated by $(1,-1)$. Quotienting the universal cover $\mathbb R^2\times I$ by this rank-one translation subgroup gives $S^1\times\mathbb R\times I$. Its first homology is $\mathbb Z$ generated by the circle. Every deck transformation is represented by a translation, and the path of translations from the identity to that translation is a homotopy, so $t$ acts as $1$. Thus the cyclic module is $\Lambda_1/(t-1)\ne0$, whereas $A_H\otimes_{\Lambda_2,\eta}\Lambda_1=0$ because $A_H=0$.

Let $G=S^1\vee S^1$ map its two based oriented loops to these meridians in $E_U$. It induces the computed fundamental-group isomorphism and intertwines abelianization to $\mathbb Z^2$. Lift it to the connected maximal abelian covers after fixing the base lift. The induced map on fundamental groups identifies the kernels of abelianization, hence is an isomorphism. Degree-one Hurewicz then makes its map on first homology an isomorphism. This is Laurent-linear: conjugation by each meridian implements its deck action on the kernel abelianization, and the map intertwines those conjugations. The same argument for total linking to $\mathbb Z$ compares the cyclic-cover $H_1$. Only first homology is compared; the separating sphere is not removed by a false homotopy equivalence. The lifted graph cellular boundary is $C_1=\Lambda_2^2\xrightarrow{(t_1-1,\ t_2-1)}C_0=\Lambda_2$, so this graph complex computes the desired first homology.

The quotient $\Lambda_2/(t_1-1)$ is $\mathbb Z[t_2^{\pm1}]$, a domain by [F5], so $t_1-1$ is prime. It does not divide $t_2-1$, whose image under $t_1\mapsto1$ is the nonzero element $t_2-1$. Under total linking, both loop edges map to $t$, so [F6] gives the cyclic-cover boundary $(t-1,t-1):\Lambda_1^2\to\Lambda_1$. Since $\Lambda_1$ is a domain, its kernel consists of $(a,-a)$ and is free of rank one. This confirms the stated cyclic-cover module and completes the example.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link (a finite disjoint union of oriented smoothly embedded circles,
[[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]) with $r\ge1$ components,
and let $X_L:=S^3\setminus L$. Then $X_L$ is a connected smooth $3$-manifold
without boundary, and in particular is path-connected, locally path-connected
and semilocally simply connected; moreover $X_L$ has the homotopy type of a
finite CW complex
([[def-cw-complex-with-closure-finiteness-and-weak-topology]]). Consequently the
covering-space classification
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]]) applies to $X_L$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f:M\to N$ be smooth and let $Z\subseteq N$ be a closed embedded
submanifold. Then $f$ is smoothly homotopic to a smooth map $g:M\to N$ with
$g\pitchfork Z$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f:M\to N$ be smooth and let $Z\subseteq N$ be a closed embedded
submanifold. Suppose $f$ is already transverse to $Z$ on an open neighbourhood
of a closed set $A\subseteq M$. Then in the transversality homotopy theorem one
can choose the perturbation family so that the perturbed map and the whole
homotopy agree with $f$ on a smaller neighbourhood of $A$.

For every path-connected topological space $X$ and $x_0\in X$, the Hurewicz map
$$h:\pi_1(X,x_0)\longrightarrow H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
is surjective and has kernel $[\pi_1(X,x_0),\pi_1(X,x_0)]$. Hence it induces a natural isomorphism
$$\pi_1(X,x_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong H_1(X;\mathbb Z).$$
The proof is choice-free and requires no CW, separation, local path-connectivity or local simple-connectivity assumption.

derivations.claim: Choose a basepoint $x_0\in X\setminus F$, which exists on a local side of any interior point of $F$. Represent any class of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ by a smooth loop transverse to $\operatorname{Int}F$, using [F2]. Define $I_F$ on that class to be its signed intersection count. If two such loops are homotopic in $X$, perturb the homotopy relative to its boundary by [F2]. The inverse image of $\operatorname{Int}F$ is then a compact oriented one-manifold in the homotopy annulus; it is compact because the annulus image is disjoint from $L=\partial F$. Orient it using the orientations of the annulus and the normal of $F$. Its oriented boundary signs at the two ends are the intersection signs of the endpoint loops with opposite signs on the two boundary circles. The total signed boundary count is zero, so the endpoint intersection counts agree. Concatenation adds counts, hence $I_F:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphism.

By [F3], this homomorphism factors through a homomorphism $\overline I_F:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$. The signed intersection convention in the Statement agrees with this induced map on the class represented by $J$.

Near a point of $K_i$, choose oriented local coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in which $K_i$ is the $x$-axis and $F$ is the half-plane $y\ge0$, $z=0$. The boundary orientation and the stated positive-meridian convention make $(x,y,z)$ ambient-positive. The small positive meridian crosses this half-plane exactly once, at $(0,\rho,0)$ for some $\rho>0$, in the $+z$ direction. Thus $\overline I_F([\mu_i])=1$ for every $i$.

By [F1], the classes $[\mu_i]$ form a basis of $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$. The homomorphisms $\overline I_F$ and $\varphi$ agree on every basis element by step 1.2 and [F1], so they are equal. Evaluating this equality on $[J]$ gives $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Every orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $g:S^2\to S^2$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth isotopy of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, stationary near its time endpoints. Consequently every smooth diffeomorphism $b:\partial B_0\to\partial B_1$ between the boundaries of two parametrized smooth $3$-balls extends to a smooth diffeomorphism $B_0\to B_1$. In the radial boundary collars supplied by their parametrizations, the extension can be required to have the product form $(x,r)\mapsto(b(x),r)$ on one smaller collar. Its orientation agrees with the orientation of $b$ on the boundaries, using the outward-normal convention.

This asserts existence of an isotopy for each given map; it does not assert a deformation retraction parametrized by the entire diffeomorphism group.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

All isotopies below are jointly smooth diffeotopies, stationary near the time endpoints.

1. On $A=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times[0,1]$, every smooth diffeomorphism fixing both boundary circles pointwise is isotopic relative to the boundary to exactly one twist
$$D_k(\theta,u)=(\theta+k\rho(u),u),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $\rho$ is a fixed smooth function equal to zero near $0$ and one near $1$. If the map initially fixes a boundary collar, a common smaller collar can be fixed throughout this isotopy. Without fixing the boundary, every annulus diffeomorphism is isotopic to one of the four maps $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,u)$ or $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,1-u)$, with $\varepsilon=\pm1$.
2. Every smooth diffeomorphism of $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ inducing the identity on $H_1(T^2;\mathbb Z)$ is smoothly isotopic to the identity. Consequently every torus diffeomorphism is smoothly isotopic to the linear torus map inducing its integral unimodular matrix on $H_1$.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact orientable smooth three-manifold and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite disjoint family of properly embedded two-sided annuli. Suppose each map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(M)$ is injective and every component of the cut-open manifold $M\mathbin{\|}\mathcal A$, with its boundary corners rounded, is irreducible. Then $M$ is irreducible. The family may be empty, and its annuli need not be separating or boundary-incompressible.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Fix an HNN extension in associated-subgroup notation and choose transversal data
$(S_-,S_+)$ as in [[def-choice-of-transversals-for-hnn-normal-forms]]. Then
every element of the HNN extension is represented by a unique transversal normal
form

$$a_0t^{\varepsilon_1}a_1\cdots t^{\varepsilon_n}a_n.$$

In particular, the identity has the unique normal form with $n=0$ and
$a_0=e_A$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

For pointed topological spaces $(X,x_0)$ and $(Y,y_0)$, the coordinate projections induce a natural group isomorphism

$$\Theta:\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0),\qquad [\gamma]\longmapsto([\pi_X\gamma],[\pi_Y\gamma]).$$

Its inverse sends $([\alpha],[\beta])$ to the class of the paired loop $s\mapsto(\alpha(s),\beta(s))$.

derivations.claim: The solid torus is irreducible. Embed it as a standard unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. A sphere in its interior has two ball sides by [F2]. Its exterior solid torus is connected and misses the sphere, so lies entirely on one side; the other ball is contained in $V$. We will use the following disk-push consequence with its smooth interpretation. If two smooth disks meet just along their common boundary and bound such a ball, their faces admit a common-boundary disk sweep through the ball. To retain the actual faces, take a thin rim collar first. At a transverse rim its normal section is a quadrant; at a previously shared collar first separate the two faces by a small normal graph. Parametrize the two faces by smooth disks with their prescribed rim collars, using [F3]. Round and truncate the rim; the remaining boundary is a smooth sphere with these marked disk and collar portions. The two disk maps and the intervening product annulus give a smooth boundary diffeomorphism to the corresponding standard rounded lens; [F3] extends it over the ball. Restore the quadrant rim using those same product collars. This gives a lens parameter retaining both faces and their rim coordinates. In this parameter use [F4]'s spherical-cap sweep; in the rim section its inward tangent runs between the two face tangents and stays nonzero. The sweep is jointly smooth, including at the disk center, by [F4]'s displayed formulas. It can be continued just past either face in its normal collar and extended ambiently by [F5]. If another surface misses the ball except in one face, the push removes that face's intersections and creates none. The support can be restricted to the ball and arbitrarily thin face and rim collars.

For the classification first replace $F$ by its neat representative using [F9]; both disk-obstruction hypotheses pass to it. Its boundary and abstract surface are unchanged. The topological ambient extension pulls a boundary-parallel product back to the original surface, and no smooth product at an original tangency is asserted. In the rest of the classification denote this neat representative again by $F$. The surface $F$ is compact, since its inclusion is proper and $V$ is compact, and it is orientable, since it is two-sided in oriented $V$. If some component $c$ of $\partial F$ is nullhomotopic on $\partial V$, choose one with an innermost boundary disk $Q$ whose interior misses all of $\partial F$. A short inward push gives a disk with boundary $c$ on $F$ and interior disjoint from $F$. If $F$ is not a disk, $c$ is essential on $F$: a boundary circle of a connected surface can bound a disk in that surface only when that disk is the entire surface, by the local half-disk charts and connectedness. The pushed disk would therefore compress $F$. Thus in this case $F$ is a disk. For the rest of the classification suppose $F$ is not a disk; then every boundary circle is essential on $\partial V$. Disjoint essential circles on a torus have the same primitive unoriented slope, as the strip reductions of [F4] show. Use those reductions for the finite family and extend into a boundary collar by [F5] to make them parallel affine circles in coordinates $(\mu,\phi)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$, where $\phi$ is the longitude coordinate of $V$. If the slope is meridional, choose a standard meridian disk $D_0$ with boundary disjoint from them. Otherwise the affine circles have nonzero $\phi$ derivative and meet $\partial D_0=\{\phi=0\}$ transversely.

Put the interiors of $F$ and $D_0$ in finite transverse position. An innermost intersection circle on $D_0$ bounds a disk $D$ with interior missing $F$. Incompressibility makes its boundary bound a disk $D'$ on $F$. The sphere $D\cup D'$ bounds a ball in $V$ by step 1.1, with the corner interpreted there. The connected surface $F\setminus\operatorname{Int}D'$ reaches $\partial V$, misses the sphere off its rim, and hence lies on the exterior side of that ball. The disk push of step 1.1 replaces $D'$ by a disk just past $D$. It removes this circle and any additional circles in $D'$, and creates none. After finitely many pushes no circle remains. The isotopies have interior support and retain the normalized boundary curves.

Suppose an intersection arc remains. An outermost arc $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D$ in $D_0$, with other boundary arc $\beta\subset\partial D_0$ and interior missing $F$. Boundary-incompressibility implies that $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D'$ on $F$, with other boundary arc $\gamma$ contained in one component of $\partial F$. If the slope were meridional there would be no arc endpoints, by the chosen disjoint boundaries. Otherwise $\gamma$ is a nonconstant subarc of an affine boundary circle whose longitude coordinate is strictly monotone on its lift. Both its endpoints have $\phi=0$, so its lifted longitude displacement is a nonzero integer. But $\beta$ has constant longitude. The union $D\cup D'$, pushed a little along its common edge if necessary, gives a continuous disk cap for the loop $\beta\cup\gamma$ in $V$. Its longitude degree would therefore be zero, contradicting that nonzero integer. Thus there are no arcs. If the slope were nonmeridional, the affine boundary curves would necessarily meet $\partial D_0$, so this case is impossible. We have made $F$ disjoint from $D_0$. Cutting $V$ along $D_0$ leaves a ball. An innermost boundary circle of $F$ on its boundary sphere has a disk there with interior missing all boundary circles of $F$. Push it inward. Unless $F$ is a disk it is a compressing disk, by the boundary-circle argument of step 2.1. This contradicts our supposition that $F$ was not a disk.

Let $D_1,D_2$ be meridian disks with the same boundary $C$. If either disk is not neat, first neatify each separately by [F9], fixing $C$. Apply the following neat-disk argument and then reverse the second embedding path. This gives a smooth embedding isotopy for the broad inputs; their two explicit topological ambient extensions and the middle smooth ambient path give a topological ambient extension. For neat inputs no preliminary change is necessary, and the entire argument below is smooth ambient. Now suppose both disks neat. In coordinates along $C$, use a small normal graph to separate their interior collars while fixing $C$ pointwise: with inward boundary coordinate $q\ge0$ and a transverse coordinate $y$ on $\partial V$, the two collars can be arranged as $y=\pm\varepsilon q$ on a common smaller strip. First each neat disk is straightened to such a graph by its full-rank collar coordinates; interpolation of the positive inward derivative gives an embedding path on a common compact strip, extended by [F5]. This keeps every boundary point fixed. General position relative to those collars then leaves only finitely many interior intersection circles. An innermost one on $D_1$ and its subdisk on $D_2$ bound a ball by irreducibility. The complement of that subdisk in $D_2$ reaches $C$ outside the ball, so the disk push from step 1.1 removes the circle and any circles inside that subdisk. Repeat until the interiors are disjoint. The resulting disks bound a ball with rim $C$, again by step 1.1 after the rim is rounded. Its common-boundary cap sweep carries one disk to the other, fixing $C$ throughout; at the rim every intermediate tangent is an inward direction between the two collar tangents, so the family remains neat in $V$. Undo the preliminary isotopies of $D_2$ and concatenate with stationary time changes. This gives a jointly smooth isotopy relative to $C$; The velocity vanishes on $C$ throughout this neat path. In a neat boundary chart it is $q$ times a smooth coefficient, as in [F9] and its neatification supplier Proof 5.2. Extend that coefficient and retain the factor $q$; the finite compact flow gives a smooth ambient isotopy fixing all of $\partial V$, not only $C$.

We have proved that $F$ is a disk. If $\partial F$ is essential on $\partial V$, it is a primitive class in the kernel of $\pi_1(\partial V)=\mathbb Z\mu\oplus\mathbb Z\phi\to\pi_1(V)=\mathbb Z\phi$, since $F$ caps it. It is therefore $\pm\mu$, so $F$ is a meridian disk. If $\partial F$ is inessential, let $Q$ be its disk on $\partial V$. The sphere $F\cup Q$, pushed slightly into the interior and rounded, bounds a ball there. Restore the boundary collar as in step 1.1 to get a ball with these two disk faces. Its marked lens parameter gives the boundary-parallel product: extend $Q$ a short distance beyond its rim in $\partial V$ and retain a smaller collar on $F$; in the normal section the two disk faces are separated by a rectangle, with its outer edge on $\partial V$. The lens parameter away from that rim and this rectangle near it identify the region with $D^2\times[0,1]$, with $D^2\times\{0\}=F$ and the other disk and lateral annulus in $\partial V$. Thus $F$ is boundary-parallel in exactly [F1]'s product sense. Conversely a boundary-parallel disk has no essential circle or essential proper arc, so it does satisfy both disk-obstruction hypotheses; this is why it must be retained in the conclusion.

Finally, if a two-sided torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ had no compressing disk, [F6] would inject $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ into $\pi_1(V)\cong\mathbb Z$. No such injection exists: for images $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ of the two generators, $(b,-a)$ is in the kernel when $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, and otherwise the entire group is the kernel. This contradiction yields a smooth compressing disk. This use of [F6] is within its compact smooth scope and does not turn a PL disk into a smooth disk without the supplied bridge. All earlier isotopies are smooth by the explicit cap, graph and finite extension constructions; the full AC assumption covers [F6] and implies the countable choice used elsewhere.

Finally allow the torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ to be TOP two-sided with its given product neighborhood, without assuming it smooth. Cut along that TOP collar. The cut pieces are compact orientable TOP3-manifolds; there are either two connected pieces with one torus face each, or one connected piece with two torus faces. Indeed every piece meets a face, and each face is connected. If any face map has nontrivial fundamental-group kernel, [F10] gives a proper disk in that cut piece whose boundary has nontrivial class on the face. Its image in $V$ is an embedded TOP compression of $T$ contained in $\operatorname{Int}V$, since its interior misses every cut boundary face and its boundary lies on only the chosen copy of $T$. Suppose therefore all face maps inject. In the two-piece case, [F11] embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in their amalgam $\pi_1(V)$. In the one-piece case choose a path in the cut piece joining the two face basepoints. Adjoining a thin copy of this path to the collar makes its overlap connected; van Kampen gives the presentation $\langle\pi_1(W),t\mid t i_+(a)t^{-1}=i_-(a),\ a\in\pi_1(T)\rangle$. One torus-overlap group maps to the collar's torus group and the other to its conjugate by the new path letter, which is exactly the displayed HNN relation. The two injected face groups are its associated subgroups, so HNN normal form [F11] again embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in $\pi_1(V)$. Both alternatives would inject $\mathbb Z^2$ into $\mathbb Z$, impossible: if the two basis images are $a,b$, then $(b,-a)$ is a nonzero kernel vector when either image is nonzero, and otherwise the whole group is the kernel. Thus some face kernel is nontrivial and the TOP compression exists. This closes the original unqualified torus clause without converting its input or its resulting disk to the smooth category. The preceding smooth classification and meridian-isotopy arguments are unchanged; their original convention/disposition remains owned by the parent assembly.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Every orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $g:S^2\to S^2$ is joined to the identity by a jointly smooth isotopy of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms, stationary near its time endpoints. Consequently every smooth diffeomorphism $b:\partial B_0\to\partial B_1$ between the boundaries of two parametrized smooth $3$-balls extends to a smooth diffeomorphism $B_0\to B_1$. In the radial boundary collars supplied by their parametrizations, the extension can be required to have the product form $(x,r)\mapsto(b(x),r)$ on one smaller collar. Its orientation agrees with the orientation of $b$ on the boundaries, using the outward-normal convention.

This asserts existence of an isotopy for each given map; it does not assert a deformation retraction parametrized by the entire diffeomorphism group.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The bounded region of a smooth embedded
circle in the oriented plane, together with its boundary, is a smooth manifold
with boundary diffeomorphic to the closed standard disk. Let $D_0,D_1$ be two
such closed regions. Every orientation-preserving smooth boundary
diffeomorphism $b:\partial D_0\to\partial D_1$ extends to an
orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $B:D_0\to D_1$. More precisely, for
specified smooth inward collars $c_i:\partial D_i\times[0,\epsilon)\to D_i$
with $c_i(p,0)=p$, the extension may be required to satisfy
$B(c_0(p,r))=c_1(b(p),r)$ for every sufficiently small $r\ge0$. In addition, given interior points $p_i\in D_i$ and an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $q$ from a neighborhood of $p_0$ onto a neighborhood of $p_1$, the extension can agree with $q$ near $p_0$ while retaining the prescribed boundary collars.

All isotopies below are jointly smooth diffeotopies, stationary near the time endpoints.

1. On $A=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times[0,1]$, every smooth diffeomorphism fixing both boundary circles pointwise is isotopic relative to the boundary to exactly one twist
$$D_k(\theta,u)=(\theta+k\rho(u),u),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $\rho$ is a fixed smooth function equal to zero near $0$ and one near $1$. If the map initially fixes a boundary collar, a common smaller collar can be fixed throughout this isotopy. Without fixing the boundary, every annulus diffeomorphism is isotopic to one of the four maps $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,u)$ or $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,1-u)$, with $\varepsilon=\pm1$.
2. Every smooth diffeomorphism of $T^2=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ inducing the identity on $H_1(T^2;\mathbb Z)$ is smoothly isotopic to the identity. Consequently every torus diffeomorphism is smoothly isotopic to the linear torus map inducing its integral unimodular matrix on $H_1$.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ be a compact orientable smooth three-manifold and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite disjoint family of properly embedded two-sided annuli. Suppose each map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(M)$ is injective and every component of the cut-open manifold $M\mathbin{\|}\mathcal A$, with its boundary corners rounded, is irreducible. Then $M$ is irreducible. The family may be empty, and its annuli need not be separating or boundary-incompressible.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

Let $F_0=f(F)$ be a compact two-sided smoothly embedded surface in a compact smooth three-manifold, with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$, and let $F_1,H_1$ be its angular neatification from [[lem-compact-smooth-boundary-preimage-surfaces-admit-neat-embedding-isotopies]]. The ambient manifold may be nonorientable. If $F_1$ has a smooth compressing disk or smooth boundary-compressing disk, then $F_0$ has a disk of the same type. Boundary-compressing disks can also be transported in the opposite direction: if $F_0$ has one, then $F_1$ has one. Consequently absence of either kind of smooth disk passes from $F_0$ to $F_1$.

Here the boundary-compressing witness has one boundary arc in the surface and the other in $\partial M$, its interior missing both. The construction allows the broader convention of ordinary smooth disk embeddings with tangential endpoint contact, and also gives smooth corner-disk witnesses with transverse surface arcs when that convention is used. No smooth ambient removal of an original surface tangency is asserted.

Assume full AC. Every compact topological three-manifold $M$, with boundary allowed, is homeomorphic to the realization of a finite combinatorial three-manifold triangulation, with boundary allowed (the empty complex when $M=\varnothing$). Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

If a TOP product collar of the boundary, together with a finite PL structure on its boundary surface, has already been supplied, the new PL structure may be chosen equal to that product PL structure on a smaller boundary neighborhood. No smooth marking or smooth ambient isotopy is asserted. Full AC remains the hypothesis of this theorem; no choice-free theorem is obtained by omitting that premise.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable piecewise linear three-manifold with a given finite compatible manifold triangulation and with boundary a subcomplex. Let $F\subset\partial M$ be a connected compact piecewise linear subsurface and $N\trianglelefteq\pi_1(F)$ a normal subgroup. Suppose there is a continuous map $f:(D^2,\partial D^2)\to(M,F)$ whose boundary lies in the relative interior of $F$ and has class outside $N$. Then there is a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$, with boundary in the relative interior of $F$, whose boundary class is outside $N$.

In particular, if a connected boundary component has noninjective induced fundamental-group map into $M$, it contains an essential simple closed curve bounding a properly embedded piecewise linear disk in $M$. Boundary classes outside $N$ are understood up to conjugation by a basepath in $F$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Fix an HNN extension in associated-subgroup notation and choose transversal data
$(S_-,S_+)$ as in [[def-choice-of-transversals-for-hnn-normal-forms]]. Then
every element of the HNN extension is represented by a unique transversal normal
form

$$a_0t^{\varepsilon_1}a_1\cdots t^{\varepsilon_n}a_n.$$

In particular, the identity has the unique normal form with $n=0$ and
$a_0=e_A$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

For pointed topological spaces $(X,x_0)$ and $(Y,y_0)$, the coordinate projections induce a natural group isomorphism

$$\Theta:\pi_1(X\times Y,(x_0,y_0))\longrightarrow\pi_1(X,x_0)\times\pi_1(Y,y_0),\qquad [\gamma]\longmapsto([\pi_X\gamma],[\pi_Y\gamma]).$$

Its inverse sends $([\alpha],[\beta])$ to the class of the paired loop $s\mapsto(\alpha(s),\beta(s))$.

derivations.claim: The solid torus is irreducible. Embed it as a standard unknotted solid torus in $S^3$. A sphere in its interior has two ball sides by [F2]. Its exterior solid torus is connected and misses the sphere, so lies entirely on one side; the other ball is contained in $V$. We will use the following disk-push consequence with its smooth interpretation. If two smooth disks meet just along their common boundary and bound such a ball, their faces admit a common-boundary disk sweep through the ball. To retain the actual faces, take a thin rim collar first. At a transverse rim its normal section is a quadrant; at a previously shared collar first separate the two faces by a small normal graph. Parametrize the two faces by smooth disks with their prescribed rim collars, using [F3]. Round and truncate the rim; the remaining boundary is a smooth sphere with these marked disk and collar portions. The two disk maps and the intervening product annulus give a smooth boundary diffeomorphism to the corresponding standard rounded lens; [F3] extends it over the ball. Restore the quadrant rim using those same product collars. This gives a lens parameter retaining both faces and their rim coordinates. In this parameter use [F4]'s spherical-cap sweep; in the rim section its inward tangent runs between the two face tangents and stays nonzero. The sweep is jointly smooth, including at the disk center, by [F4]'s displayed formulas. It can be continued just past either face in its normal collar and extended ambiently by [F5]. If another surface misses the ball except in one face, the push removes that face's intersections and creates none. The support can be restricted to the ball and arbitrarily thin face and rim collars.

For the classification first replace $F$ by its neat representative using [F9]; both disk-obstruction hypotheses pass to it. Its boundary and abstract surface are unchanged. The topological ambient extension pulls a boundary-parallel product back to the original surface, and no smooth product at an original tangency is asserted. In the rest of the classification denote this neat representative again by $F$. The surface $F$ is compact, since its inclusion is proper and $V$ is compact, and it is orientable, since it is two-sided in oriented $V$. If some component $c$ of $\partial F$ is nullhomotopic on $\partial V$, choose one with an innermost boundary disk $Q$ whose interior misses all of $\partial F$. A short inward push gives a disk with boundary $c$ on $F$ and interior disjoint from $F$. If $F$ is not a disk, $c$ is essential on $F$: a boundary circle of a connected surface can bound a disk in that surface only when that disk is the entire surface, by the local half-disk charts and connectedness. The pushed disk would therefore compress $F$. Thus in this case $F$ is a disk. For the rest of the classification suppose $F$ is not a disk; then every boundary circle is essential on $\partial V$. Disjoint essential circles on a torus have the same primitive unoriented slope, as the strip reductions of [F4] show. Use those reductions for the finite family and extend into a boundary collar by [F5] to make them parallel affine circles in coordinates $(\mu,\phi)\in(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2$, where $\phi$ is the longitude coordinate of $V$. If the slope is meridional, choose a standard meridian disk $D_0$ with boundary disjoint from them. Otherwise the affine circles have nonzero $\phi$ derivative and meet $\partial D_0=\{\phi=0\}$ transversely.

Finally, if a two-sided torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ had no compressing disk, [F6] would inject $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ into $\pi_1(V)\cong\mathbb Z$. No such injection exists: for images $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ of the two generators, $(b,-a)$ is in the kernel when $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$, and otherwise the entire group is the kernel. This contradiction yields a smooth compressing disk. This use of [F6] is within its compact smooth scope and does not turn a PL disk into a smooth disk without the supplied bridge. All earlier isotopies are smooth by the explicit cap, graph and finite extension constructions; the full AC assumption covers [F6] and implies the countable choice used elsewhere.

Put the interiors of $F$ and $D_0$ in finite transverse position. An innermost intersection circle on $D_0$ bounds a disk $D$ with interior missing $F$. Incompressibility makes its boundary bound a disk $D'$ on $F$. The sphere $D\cup D'$ bounds a ball in $V$ by step 1.1, with the corner interpreted there. The connected surface $F\setminus\operatorname{Int}D'$ reaches $\partial V$, misses the sphere off its rim, and hence lies on the exterior side of that ball. The disk push of step 1.1 replaces $D'$ by a disk just past $D$. It removes this circle and any additional circles in $D'$, and creates none. After finitely many pushes no circle remains. The isotopies have interior support and retain the normalized boundary curves.

Suppose an intersection arc remains. An outermost arc $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D$ in $D_0$, with other boundary arc $\beta\subset\partial D_0$ and interior missing $F$. Boundary-incompressibility implies that $\alpha$ cuts off a disk $D'$ on $F$, with other boundary arc $\gamma$ contained in one component of $\partial F$. If the slope were meridional there would be no arc endpoints, by the chosen disjoint boundaries. Otherwise $\gamma$ is a nonconstant subarc of an affine boundary circle whose longitude coordinate is strictly monotone on its lift. Both its endpoints have $\phi=0$, so its lifted longitude displacement is a nonzero integer. But $\beta$ has constant longitude. The union $D\cup D'$, pushed a little along its common edge if necessary, gives a continuous disk cap for the loop $\beta\cup\gamma$ in $V$. Its longitude degree would therefore be zero, contradicting that nonzero integer. Thus there are no arcs. If the slope were nonmeridional, the affine boundary curves would necessarily meet $\partial D_0$, so this case is impossible. We have made $F$ disjoint from $D_0$. Cutting $V$ along $D_0$ leaves a ball. An innermost boundary circle of $F$ on its boundary sphere has a disk there with interior missing all boundary circles of $F$. Push it inward. Unless $F$ is a disk it is a compressing disk, by the boundary-circle argument of step 2.1. This contradicts our supposition that $F$ was not a disk.

Let $D_1,D_2$ be meridian disks with the same boundary $C$. If either disk is not neat, first neatify each separately by [F9], fixing $C$. Apply the following neat-disk argument and then reverse the second embedding path. This gives a smooth embedding isotopy for the broad inputs; their two explicit topological ambient extensions and the middle smooth ambient path give a topological ambient extension. For neat inputs no preliminary change is necessary, and the entire argument below is smooth ambient. Now suppose both disks neat. In coordinates along $C$, use a small normal graph to separate their interior collars while fixing $C$ pointwise: with inward boundary coordinate $q\ge0$ and a transverse coordinate $y$ on $\partial V$, the two collars can be arranged as $y=\pm\varepsilon q$ on a common smaller strip. First each neat disk is straightened to such a graph by its full-rank collar coordinates; interpolation of the positive inward derivative gives an embedding path on a common compact strip, extended by [F5]. This keeps every boundary point fixed. General position relative to those collars then leaves only finitely many interior intersection circles. An innermost one on $D_1$ and its subdisk on $D_2$ bound a ball by irreducibility. The complement of that subdisk in $D_2$ reaches $C$ outside the ball, so the disk push from step 1.1 removes the circle and any circles inside that subdisk. Repeat until the interiors are disjoint. The resulting disks bound a ball with rim $C$, again by step 1.1 after the rim is rounded. Its common-boundary cap sweep carries one disk to the other, fixing $C$ throughout; at the rim every intermediate tangent is an inward direction between the two collar tangents, so the family remains neat in $V$. Undo the preliminary isotopies of $D_2$ and concatenate with stationary time changes. This gives a jointly smooth isotopy relative to $C$; The velocity vanishes on $C$ throughout this neat path. In a neat boundary chart it is $q$ times a smooth coefficient, as in [F9] and its neatification supplier Proof 5.2. Extend that coefficient and retain the factor $q$; the finite compact flow gives a smooth ambient isotopy fixing all of $\partial V$, not only $C$.

We have proved that $F$ is a disk. If $\partial F$ is essential on $\partial V$, it is a primitive class in the kernel of $\pi_1(\partial V)=\mathbb Z\mu\oplus\mathbb Z\phi\to\pi_1(V)=\mathbb Z\phi$, since $F$ caps it. It is therefore $\pm\mu$, so $F$ is a meridian disk. If $\partial F$ is inessential, let $Q$ be its disk on $\partial V$. The sphere $F\cup Q$, pushed slightly into the interior and rounded, bounds a ball there. Restore the boundary collar as in step 1.1 to get a ball with these two disk faces. Its marked lens parameter gives the boundary-parallel product: extend $Q$ a short distance beyond its rim in $\partial V$ and retain a smaller collar on $F$; in the normal section the two disk faces are separated by a rectangle, with its outer edge on $\partial V$. The lens parameter away from that rim and this rectangle near it identify the region with $D^2\times[0,1]$, with $D^2\times\{0\}=F$ and the other disk and lateral annulus in $\partial V$. Thus $F$ is boundary-parallel in exactly [F1]'s product sense. Conversely a boundary-parallel disk has no essential circle or essential proper arc, so it does satisfy both disk-obstruction hypotheses; this is why it must be retained in the conclusion.

Finally allow the torus $T\subset\operatorname{Int}V$ to be TOP two-sided with its given product neighborhood, without assuming it smooth. Cut along that TOP collar. The cut pieces are compact orientable TOP3-manifolds; there are either two connected pieces with one torus face each, or one connected piece with two torus faces. Indeed every piece meets a face, and each face is connected. If any face map has nontrivial fundamental-group kernel, [F10] gives a proper disk in that cut piece whose boundary has nontrivial class on the face. Its image in $V$ is an embedded TOP compression of $T$ contained in $\operatorname{Int}V$, since its interior misses every cut boundary face and its boundary lies on only the chosen copy of $T$. Suppose therefore all face maps inject. In the two-piece case, [F11] embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in their amalgam $\pi_1(V)$. In the one-piece case choose a path in the cut piece joining the two face basepoints. Adjoining a thin copy of this path to the collar makes its overlap connected; van Kampen gives the presentation $\langle\pi_1(W),t\mid t i_+(a)t^{-1}=i_-(a),\ a\in\pi_1(T)\rangle$. One torus-overlap group maps to the collar's torus group and the other to its conjugate by the new path letter, which is exactly the displayed HNN relation. The two injected face groups are its associated subgroups, so HNN normal form [F11] again embeds $\pi_1(T)$ in $\pi_1(V)$. Both alternatives would inject $\mathbb Z^2$ into $\mathbb Z$, impossible: if the two basis images are $a,b$, then $(b,-a)$ is a nonzero kernel vector when either image is nonzero, and otherwise the whole group is the kernel. Thus some face kernel is nontrivial and the TOP compression exists. This closes the original unqualified torus clause without converting its input or its resulting disk to the smooth category. The preceding smooth classification and meridian-isotopy arguments are unchanged; their original convention/disposition remains owned by the parent assembly.
