The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a four-dimensional manifold with boundary and let $W$ be a compact surface with boundary. An embedding $e:(W,\partial W)\to(X,\partial X)$ is proper when $e^{-1}(\partial X)=\partial W$. It is locally flat at an interior point of $W$ when there are neighborhoods of the point and its image and a homeomorphism of pairs from those neighborhoods to $(\mathbb R^4,\mathbb R^2)$, with the standard linear plane $\mathbb R^2\subset\mathbb R^4$. It is locally flat at a boundary point when there are such neighborhoods and a homeomorphism of pairs to $(\mathbb R^4_+,\mathbb R^2_+)$, where $\mathbb R^4_+=\{x_4\geq0\}$ and $\mathbb R^2_+=\{x_2=x_3=0,\ x_4\geq0\}$; the line $\partial\mathbb R^2_+$ lies in $\partial\mathbb R^4_+$. A collar of a boundary circle of $W$ is an embedding of that circle times $[0,\varepsilon)$ into $W$ that is the identity on the circle at parameter $0$; a concordance collar is required to agree with the corresponding product collar of the ambient end. A smooth proper surface has the analogous smooth charts and collars, which are also topological locally flat charts.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, and let $X_t$ be a smooth
time-dependent vector field on $M$ over $I$. For every $(s,p)\in I\times M$
there exist an open interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$, open
neighbourhoods $U_r$ of the evolving points, and a smooth map

$$ \Psi:\{(t,s,q): t,s\in J,\ q\in U_s\}\to M $$

such that $t\mapsto \Psi_{t,s}(q)$ is the unique solution of
$\dot\gamma(t)=X_t(\gamma(t))$ with $\Psi_{s,s}(q)=q$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:M\to\mathbb R^k$ be continuous, where $M$ is a smooth manifold, and let $\varepsilon:M\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive continuous error function. Then there exists a smooth map $\widetilde F:M\to\mathbb R^k$ such that
$$\|\widetilde F(p)-F(p)\|<\varepsilon(p)\qquad\text{for all }p\in M.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every compact smooth manifold, with boundary
allowed, has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. If its boundary is a
supplied finite CW manifold, the collar may be retained in a finite relative CW
model.

Let $\mathcal L$ be one local system on $X$.

1. If $Z\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, inclusion induces excision isomorphisms in both local homology and local cohomology between $(X\setminus Z,A\setminus Z)$ and $(X,A)$, using the restrictions of $\mathcal L$.
2. For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, there are natural exact sequences
   $$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H_n(V;\mathcal L)\to H_n(X;\mathcal L)\to\cdots$$
   and
   $$\cdots\to H^n(X;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U;\mathcal L)\oplus H^n(V;\mathcal L)\to H^n(U\cap V;\mathcal L)\to\cdots,$$
   where all systems are restrictions and the middle difference map in cohomology is $u|_{U\cap V}-v|_{U\cap V}$.

The same conclusions hold for the standard excisive-cover condition after replacing the cover by interiors. A local system given only on a subspace is not silently assumed to extend to $X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

Assume AC. Fix the usual orientation of $S^n$. If $K$ is a nonempty proper compact weakly locally contractible subspace of $S^n$ and $R$ is a commutative unital ring, there are isomorphisms
$$\widetilde H_i(S^n\setminus K;R)\cong\widetilde H^{n-i-1}(K;R)$$
for every integer $i$. They are natural for inclusions of such compact subsets, with the reverse inclusions of their complements, and with the fixed sphere orientation.

For the nonempty spaces here, reduced homology in degree zero is the augmentation kernel, reduced cohomology in degree zero is the quotient by constant classes, positive reduced groups are ordinary groups, and negative reduced groups are zero. AC is inherited from Poincaré duality and the neighborhood-retract theorem.

If $M$ is a compact topological manifold with boundary $A=\partial M$, there is an open neighborhood $V$ of $A$ and a homeomorphism
$$c:A\times[0,1)\xrightarrow{\sim}V,\qquad c(x,0)=x.$$
Consequently $A\hookrightarrow M$ is an unbased cofibration, and $M\setminus A\hookrightarrow M$ is a homotopy equivalence. The manifold is Hausdorff and second countable by convention. All three conclusions require no AC.

derivations.claim: Use the given boundary product collar to extend $D$ a little beyond $S^3$. Its normal quotient planes are represented by smooth orthogonal projection matrices $Q$ in the ambient Euclidean space. Parametrize the original disk radially from one interior point. Along each radial segment solve $\dot U=[\dot Q,Q]U$ from one fixed oriented orthonormal frame. The skew-symmetric coefficient preserves norms, and compactness gives a bounded coefficient on the finite parameter disk and time interval, so the local solutions of [F2] extend over the entire interval and depend smoothly on the endpoint. This gives a smooth frame of the disk's normal quotient bundle. Choose an ambient metric product-shaped on the end collar, by a one-variable cutoff interpolation with its product metric. Its orthogonal normal bundle is isomorphic to the quotient and inherits the frame. Its geodesic map is the local flow of the smooth coordinate equation $\ddot x^k=-\tfrac12g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_jg_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij})\dot x^i\dot x^j$, whose transformation rule follows by the chain rule. At the zero section its derivative adds tangent and normal vectors, hence is invertible. Extend across the end collar and apply [F2] there. Compactness of the original disk gives a uniform injective tube radius: otherwise equal images of distinct normal vectors tending to zero have convergent basepoints, their limits are equal, and the local inverse at that zero vector is contradicted. Shrink also inside all local flow domains. This constructs an actual smooth disk tube $D^2\times D^2$, product-shaped at its boundary.

A small nonzero constant frame vector gives a disjoint proper parallel disk $D'$. By [F3], the linking of its boundary with $K$ equals $D\mathbin\cdot D'=0$. Hence the tube's induced boundary framing is precisely the preferred zero framing. Remove its interior and round the product corners to obtain the actual compact smooth disk exterior $X$. In the decomposition $B^4=X\cup(D^2\times D^2)$ the overlap retracts to $D^2\times S^1$. Since the ball and tube are contractible, integral Mayer–Vietoris gives $H_1(X)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ and $H_i(X)=0$ for $i>1$. Its marked boundary is the zero surgery $M(K)=E_K\cup_{T^2}(D^2\times S^1)$, with the disk meridian the zero longitude and the circle the positive meridian. The boundary meridian therefore induces an $H_1$ isomorphism to $X$.

We construct a boundary circle map with the actual prescribed fiber, rather than presuming that $K$ is fibered. Truncate $F$ at the knot tube to a proper surface in $E_K$, and cap its boundary with $D^2\times\{1\}$ in the inner solid torus. Call the resulting closed connected surface $\Sigma_0\subset M(K)$. Give a small normal product of $F$ the signed coordinate $u$ whose positive direction is the positive Seifert push, and put $f_0=\exp(2\pi i u)$ there. On the inner $D^2\times S^1$ put $f_0(x,z)=z$, matching these choices in the peripheral collar. Cut the rest of the knot exterior along that product of $F$. Its two faces have real phase values $\epsilon$ and $1-\epsilon$, and its remaining torus annulus has the ordinary lifted angular coordinate between them. These prescriptions agree in their product corner collars. Extend the real phase to the remaining compact cut manifold by finite smooth collar cutoffs and a partition of unity, with all values in $(0,1)$ and constant $1/2$ away from its prescribed boundary collars. Convexity keeps the extended values away from $0$ modulo $1$. Exponentiating gives a smooth map $f_0:M(K)\to S^1$ with $1$ as a regular value, fiber exactly $\Sigma_0$, and positive coorientation on the $F$ part. Its induced homomorphism on $H_1$ is the positive meridian map: crossing $F$ once positively increases the lifted phase by one, exactly the intersection convention in [F4].

Now let $D$ be the arbitrary locally flat disk of the Statement. First construct the actual boundary germ. The smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ has an oriented normal two-plane tube $\tau:K\times D^2_\delta\to S^3$: take the positive normal of the given smooth Seifert surface along $K$, complete it by the orientations of $K,S^3$, and use a uniformly small smooth tube over the compact circle, by the smooth inverse-chart/ODE construction [F2]. The matched disk and ambient product collars in the Given identify $D$ there with $K\times[0,\epsilon)\subset S^3\times[0,\epsilon)$. Thus $(q,t,v)\mapsto(\tau(q,v),t)$ is an ACTUAL rank-two normal-bundle germ over the entire boundary collar. No global TOP bundle is inferred from the Definition alone. Double the standard ball and the collared disk to $(Y,N)=(S^4,D_+\cup_KD_-)$, where $N\cong S^2$. The tube doubles to the explicit product germ $K\times(-2a,2a)\times D^2_\delta$ for small $a>0$. Choose the CLOSED seam annulus $C=K\times[-a,a]\subset N$. This is the prescribed bundle on a neighborhood of $C$; restrict its fiber radius inside a slightly larger tube for the extendable-neighborhood convention. The doubled pair is locally flat: away from the seam use the given charts; at the seam its actual product chart is $(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\{0\})$. Every hypothesis of [F6] is now literal. The ambient $S^4$ is a boundaryless smooth manifold and hence an ANR homology four-manifold; $Y\setminus N$ is an open four-manifold. The surface $N$ is closed, $N\times\mathbb R\cong S^2\times\mathbb R$ is a manifold and $\partial N=\varnothing$. Nested flat charts have complement homotopy type $S^1$; the local meridian maps give the infinite cyclic local fundamental group, and local $\pi_2=0$. Thus even the stronger condition in the reformatted erratum holds. The actual prescribed bundle near $C$ is the displayed product. Apply [F6] to obtain a normal vector bundle on $N$ whose embedding AGREES with that product on a smaller neighborhood of $C$. Restrict to $D_+$. Near its boundary, agreement with the germ keeps the collar coordinate $t$ unchanged, so sufficiently short fibers stay in the original hemisphere. Away from a smaller seam collar, the zero section is a compact subset of the interior of that hemisphere; continuity and compactness give a uniform fiber radius whose image stays there. Choose a bundle norm equal to the product norm near the seam and shrink to the smaller of those radii. This gives an actual disk tube wholly in the original $B^4$, agreeing with the prescribed product on a smaller entire boundary collar. Relative agreement, not existence of some unspecified doubled tube, justifies restriction. Its oriented rank-two vector bundle over the disk is trivial. A global nonzero frame section gives a disjoint proper parallel disk, so its boundary has linking zero with $K$ by [F3]. Thus the induced boundary framing is the preferred zero framing. Any difference from the supplied zero-framed boundary trivialization has degree zero in $SO(2)$ and extends across the disk; adjust the global frame by that extension, and restrict the actual bundle neighborhood. This gives an actual framed TOP disk tube, with the prescribed product and angular marking on a smaller boundary collar. Its compact exterior $X$ is a TOP four-manifold. The same collared decomposition and integral Mayer–Vietoris calculation as in step2.1 give $H_1(X)=\mathbb Z[\mu]$, $H_i(X)=0$ for $i>1$, with boundary the actual zero surgery $M(K)$ and its marked inner $D^2\times S^1$. No smoothing of the disk or exterior is asserted.

The same meridian class on $X$ is represented by a continuous map $g:X\to S^1$. To construct it, use the finite CW model of [F3]: send a maximal tree to the basepoint, the remaining one-cells to loops of the stipulated integer degrees, fill each two-cell because its relator has degree zero, and fill higher cells because the universal cover $\mathbb R$ of the circle is contractible. Transport the map by the actual homotopy model. The boundary homomorphism of $g$ equals that of $f_0$ by step 2.1. Smooth $g$ by viewing it in $\mathbb R^2$, extending constantly across boundary collars to the smooth double, applying [F2] within error $1/4$ and projecting the result radially to $S^1$. Normalized straight-line interpolation preserves its homotopy class. The smooth boundary ratio $f_0/g$ has zero degree on every loop, so it has a global smooth real argument: lift its argument along paths from a fixed point; zero loop increments make it path-independent, and local arguments prove smoothness. First make $g$ constant in a smaller boundary collar by a smooth reparametrization of the collar depth. Multiplication there by the exponential of the lifted boundary argument times a cutoff changes $g$ to a smooth $f:X\to S^1$ equal to $f_0$ on that smaller entire collar.

Construct on the actual boundary $M(K)$ the circle map $f_0$ of step3.1. Its knot-exterior part uses the given smooth $F$ and its positive Seifert collar; the solid-torus part is the actual framed tube's angular coordinate $f_0(x,z)=z$. Their zero-longitude boundary products agree by step8.1. The real-phase extension on the cut knot exterior stays in $(0,1)$, so the fiber over1 is exactly the capped surface $\Sigma_0$, with its prescribed whole product neighborhood and positive coorientation. On a collar of $\partial X$, extend $f_0$ constantly in collar depth. This is an actual TOP product-transverse boundary map even though it need not be smooth for the inherited structure of the original disk complement.

Make $1$ a regular value in the remaining compact interior while keeping that collar fixed. Cover the compact critical set on the fiber by finitely many interior charts with bumps positive on smaller cores. For small parameters $a_j$, the family $f_a=f\exp(2\pi i\sum_j a_j\phi_j)$ has derivative spanning the circle tangent in some parameter direction at each such core. Off these cores the original fiber map is already transverse, and sufficiently small parameters preserve that property by compactness and the inverse-function local rank criterion. Thus the total family is transverse to $1$. Parametric transversality [F2] supplies an arbitrarily small parameter with transverse slice. It is unchanged on the retained boundary collar. Its inverse image $R_0$ is a compact smooth oriented three-manifold with product boundary $\partial R_0=\Sigma_0$; orient it with the normal-last product convention so that its boundary has the stated orientation of $\Sigma_0$. Since $\Sigma_0$ is connected, exactly one component of $R_0$ meets it; discard all closed components.

The meridian class in $H^1(X;\mathbb Z)$ has a continuous circle representative by [F8]. Its boundary class equals that of $f_0$ by step8.1. The boundary ratio therefore has a continuous real argument: lift along paths, with zero increments around every loop. First make the representative constant in a smaller boundary collar by reparametrizing collar depth, then multiply there by the exponential of that argument times a collar cutoff. This constructs a continuous $f:X\to S^1$ equal to $f_0$ on a whole smaller boundary collar. The argument uses [F8] only for a continuous map; no regular value is inferred from it or from Alexander duality.

On the inner tube boundary the fiber is exactly $D^2\times\{1\}$ and is product-shaped in its normal collar, so attach the radial product $D^2\times[0,r]$ down that fixed angle to the zero section $D$. At the common peripheral circle it joins the original $F$ collar; their quadrant coordinates agree with the zero-longitude marking in step 2.1. Round these product sectors. The result is a compact connected smooth embedded $R$ with boundary the rounded capped surface $F\cup_K(-D)$, with $F$ carrying its original orientation. Here, as in the Statement's collar adjustment, use a small collar embedding of the ball into its interior and the corresponding rounding to regard the capped closed surface and its spanning $R$ as interior representatives. This retains their identification with $F\cup_KD$ and all old $F$ homology curves; it does not leave an interior point of a closed capped surface on the outer boundary. The normal coorientation of $R_0$ on $F$ was the positive Seifert direction in step 3.1, so after the same collar transport the positive push-off lies on that complementary side of $R$.

Apply [F7] in $Y=X\times S^1$ to the proper graph $M=\{(x,f(x)):x\in X\}$ and the proper submanifold $Z=X\times\{1\}$ with its specified trivial circle-normal line microbundle. Choose nested closed product collars $C_0\subset\operatorname{Int}C$ of $\partial X$ in the boundary collar where step8.3 fixes $f=f_0$, use $C$ as Quinn's protected set, and take the theorem's $D=Y$. The graph is already microbundle transverse near $C$ by step8.2. The closure of $(Y\setminus C)\cap M\cap Z$ is disjoint from $C_0$, so choose the theorem's support neighborhood disjoint from $C_0$. The isotopy may meet the outer frontier of $C$ but leaves the smaller collar $C_0$ fixed, preserving the whole boundary product and coorientation needed below. Parametrize its resulting graph image by $j_1:X\to M'$. It need not remain a graph over $X$: define instead $f'=\operatorname{pr}_{S^1}j_1$. Microbundle transversality says $R_0=(f')^{-1}(1)$ is a compact neat TOP three-manifold, with $\partial R_0=\Sigma_0$ and exactly the unchanged boundary product/coorientation. Its normal microbundle is the pullback of the specified trivial line, hence has an actual oriented product neighborhood after uniform shrinking over the compact fiber. The trivialization is the already prescribed one near the boundary. Orient $R_0$ by this normal direction and discard closed components; since $\Sigma_0$ is connected, exactly one component meets it. This is the required separate marked angular regular-fiber operation, using [F7], rather than a consequence claimed from [F6].

Finally the orientations of $R$ and of the four-ball supply a continuous unit smooth normal field on $R$. Extend it in finitely many coordinate neighborhoods by smooth cutoffs to an ambient smooth vector field. Along its small-time flow, the derivative in the normal/time direction together with the tangent directions is invertible at time zero. Local inverse charts, extended a little across the boundary collar of $R$, and compactness give one injective product $R\times[-\delta,\delta]$ in the ambient ball; the same convergent-basepoint contradiction as in step 1.1 proves injectivity after a uniform shrinking. Choose its positive direction to be the coorientation fixed on $F$. This gives the required oriented two-sided ambient product and positive-push compatibility. Thus the entire Seifert-hypersurface conclusion is proved when the supplied disk is smooth.

Attach the actual radial sector $D^2\times[0,r]$ at the fixed angular value down to the disk zero section, as in step6.1. The TOP tube products, zero-longitude peripheral marking and unchanged whole fiber collar make the attaching maps identical on their common products. In the disk's normal plane this sector is the positive coordinate ray; its transverse Cartesian coordinate supplies its two-sided normal product even at the zero-section boundary. It agrees with the angular coorientation for positive radius and with the positive Seifert normal along $F$. Round the product corners in these explicit two-dimensional sector coordinates. They paste with the product of $R_0$ from step8.4, giving the actual compact connected oriented locally flat $R$ with the stated two-sided product and positive-push alignment. Before the collar push this is the model meeting the outer sphere along $F$; the same collar embedding of the ball used in step6.1 gives the closed interior representative of $F\cup_KD$, retaining all marked $F$ homology curves and its normal direction. Together with the preserved smooth proof this proves the entire Statement under its full AC hypothesis. The normal-bundle and transversality theorems remain explicitly external inputs.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, for a commutative unital ring $R$. Cap with its relative fundamental class gives isomorphisms, for every integer $p$,
$$S_p:H^p(M;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M,A;R),\qquad T_p:H^p(M,A;R)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{n-p}(M;R).$$
Here both maps send a class $a$ to $a\cap[M,A]$ in the displayed target. Empty boundary recovers Poincaré duality. Disconnected and empty manifolds are included. AC is inherited only from the exhaustion and local universal-coefficient arguments in Poincaré duality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be disjoint finite rational $1$-cycles in the boundary $S^3$ of the standard oriented $4$-ball $B^4$, each represented as a finite rational linear combination of oriented knots. Let $P$ and $Q$ be finite rational $2$-chains in $B^4$ with $\partial P=\alpha$ and $\partial Q=\beta$, with common standard product collars at their respective boundaries and with their interiors in general position. Then the signed interior intersection number $P\cdot Q$ equals the bilinear extension of the linking number $\operatorname{lk}(\alpha,\beta)$ defined by positive meridians in $S^3$.

Let $H$ be a free abelian group of rank $2g$ and let $V:H\times H\to\mathbb Z$ be a bilinear form. Write $H_{\mathbb Q}=H\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ and extend $V$ $\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to $H_{\mathbb Q}$. If $L\subset H_{\mathbb Q}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of dimension $g$ and $V(x,y)=0$ for all $x,y\in L$, then $M=H\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand of $H$ and $V|_{M\times M}=0$.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a locally flat properly embedded disk in the standard four-ball $B^4$ with boundary an oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected oriented Seifert surface for $K$. in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Assume full AC. Its boundary is the realization of a subcomplex. Thus $M$ admits a finite compatible PL structure, without any previously supplied smooth or PL structure on its interior.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be any ordered integral basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ with Seifert matrix $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Capping the sole boundary circle of $F$ by a disk does not change $H_1$ because that circle is already the boundary of the oriented fundamental $2$-chain of $F$; by [F9] and exactness [F10], $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\cong H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. In the pair sequence [F10], $H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_0(R;\mathbb Q)$ is an isomorphism because both are connected. Exactness therefore makes $H_1(R;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)$ surjective. By [F2] and [F14], the target has dimension $b_2(R)$, so the image of $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $b_1(R)-b_2(R)$.

Let $\widehat R$ be the double of $R$ along $\Sigma$, with the second copy oppositely oriented so the orientations glue. Its two copies have open collar thickenings with intersection retracting to $\Sigma$, so [F11] gives $\chi(\widehat R)=2\chi(R)-\chi(\Sigma)$. By [F12] and [F13], $\chi(\widehat R)=0$, and by [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$; hence $\chi(R)=1-g$. Also [F2] gives $H_3(R;\mathbb Q)\cong H^0(R,\Sigma;\mathbb Q)=0$: a relative zero-cocycle is locally constant on the connected $R$ and vanishes on the nonempty connected $\Sigma$, so it is zero. With $b_0(R)=1$, the rational Euler-characteristic identity [F13] implies $b_1(R)-b_2(R)=g$. Thus the kernel $L=\ker(H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$, identified with a subspace of $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$, has dimension $2g-g=g$.

Let $x,y\in L$, represented by finite rational smooth cycles on $F$ away from $K$. Their rational bounding chains in $R$ can be taken smooth. Indeed [F6] first supplies finite smooth real bounding chains; their boundary equations are one finite rational linear system on the real coefficients of finitely many smooth simplices, so rational Gaussian elimination supplies rational coefficients solving the same equations. Use the pre-collar-push model in [F5] to place the boundary cycles back on the actual $F\subset S^3$. A finite intrinsic collar push moves the interiors of their bounding chains off the boundary of $R$, fixing the prescribed boundary collars, so the chains miss the product corner $K$. The model is smooth on a neighborhood of these compact supports. Its positive normal field is tangent to $S^3$ along $F$ and points in the positive Seifert direction; extend it by finitely many bumps to an ambient field tangent to $S^3$ there. Its small-time flow pushes the first bounding chain $X$ off $R$, with boundary exactly $x^+$ in $S^3$, while the second chain $Y$ stays in $R$ with boundary $y$. Compactness and the product neighborhood keep the two supports disjoint. Their common standard end collars and empty intersection make them admissible for [F3], so $\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)=X^+\mathbin\cdot Y=0$. By [F1] this is $V_{\mathbb Q}(x,y)$. Hence $L$ is a rational Seifert-isotropic subspace.

For the arbitrary locally flat disk use the TOP $R$ and its actual product from [F5]. The duality and pair-sequence computation of steps 1.1, 2.1 applies to this compact oriented TOP three-manifold: [F7] supplies finite homology and [F13] gives its Euler-characteristic formula, [F2] applies in the TOP category, and [F11]–[F12] give the double's Euler characteristic. By [F9], $\chi(\Sigma)=2-2g$ and $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $2g$. Thus, without putting a smooth structure on the embedding, the rational kernel $L=\ker(H_1(F;\mathbb Q)\to H_1(R;\mathbb Q))$ has dimension $g$.

By [F4], $M=H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\cap L$ is a rank-$g$ direct summand and $V|_{M\times M}=0$. By [F8], $(H_1(F;\mathbb Z),V)$ is an integral Seifert lattice; the metabolic-form definition therefore makes $M$ a metabolizer. This proves the entire metabolic conclusion whenever the supplied slice disk is smooth.

Represent $x,y\in L$ by finite rational smooth cycles in the given $F$, away from $K$, and choose finite rational CONTINUOUS bounding chains in $R$. Use its pre-collar-push model and the actual positive normal product of [F5]. Push the first chain into the positive complementary side, with boundary the actual positive Seifert push $x^+$; leave the second chain in $R$ with boundary $y$. An intrinsic boundary-collar push of their interiors and the common product near $F$ give the usual collared bounding chains in $B^4$, missing the corner $K$. Their supports are disjoint compact sets by the actual two-sided product. Choose disjoint relatively open smooth ambient neighborhoods $U,V\subset B^4$ of those supports, including their boundary cycles; these are smooth manifolds with boundary as open subsets of the standard smooth ball. In $U$, [F6] makes the smooth cycle $x^+$ bound a finite smooth real chain, since it bounds continuously there; likewise $y$ bounds in $V$. In each finite set of occurring simplices the equations for the boundary coefficients are rational, so rational Gaussian elimination replaces the real coefficients by rational ones without enlarging support. Near $S^3$, move the interiors inward and attach the standard product of the fixed boundary cycle with the collar interval. citations.quote: Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On oriented ambient-isotopy classes of smooth knots in $S^3$, the connected-sum operation is associative and commutative, and the standard unknot is a two-sided identity. Here “commutative monoid” means a set with an associative binary operation, a two-sided identity, and equality after interchanging the two inputs.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Specialize the TOP/exotic external assertion [F5] at each finite list of knot representatives and witnessing annuli actually used. For TOP these lie in the standard product; for exotic concordance the supplied boundary-marked homeomorphism to that product is part of the input code. The finite chart and pair-chart extraction in [F6] uses compactness, not a choice of an atlas for a countable family. Inside $L[r]$ use the ordinary CDR group operation, retain the actual output annulus and marked product homeomorphism, and export their compact forward/inverse and collar certificates. This proves the required finite compatibility and transitivity instances in $V$. Since each instance starts with its own given finite data, no simultaneous choice of representatives or witnesses for all classes is made. The quotient group operations and laws follow by universal quantification over these instances; the original $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis is therefore respected, rather than inferred from the unqualified source assertion. The localized category is handled directly by the subsequent homology calculations, with no TOP normal theorem needed.

The supplied connected-sum theorem gives associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity at the level of oriented knot types. The retained standard smooth boundary-sum construction on witnessing annuli gives concordance compatibility in the standard smooth product; the TOP/exotic compatibility is the external input [F5], and the localized ambient verification is given by the subsequent homology calculations. The knot-type isotopies themselves are admissible annuli in every category.

Let $D\subset B^4$ be the smooth ribbon disk for $K\#K^\dagger$ supplied by [F2]. By local smooth coordinates and straightening of the embedded disk, choose an ambiently standard interior 4-ball $B$ such that $B\cap D$ is a standard 2-disk. An ambient isotopy supported in the interior carries $B$ to a concentric standard ball, so its complement in $B^4$ is diffeomorphic to $S^3\times I$. Removing $\operatorname{int}B$ from $B^4$ and the interior of $B\cap D$ from $D$ gives a smooth annulus. The outer and inner boundary collars give product collars for it. Order the ends with $K\#K^\dagger$ at the lower end and the inner standard unknot at the upper end, and orient the annulus so its boundary is $-(K\#K^\dagger)$ at the lower end and $U$ at the upper end. It is therefore an admissible inverse concordance in the smooth category, and the same product annulus satisfies the TOP, exotic and localized ambient conditions.

The external input [F5] supplies the TOP and exotic ambient gluing/compatibility assertions at exactly the definitions in [F1]. For the localized smooth category, transitivity is stacking along the marked $S^3$: Mayer–Vietoris and the two boundary homology isomorphisms give another $R_n$-homology $S^3\times I$. Reflection gives symmetry and a product gives reflexivity, all with their smooth annulus collars.

For localized connected sum choose a smooth product neighborhood $D^3\times I$ of a proper spanning arc inside each witnessing annulus, with the annulus strip in its standard local position, and remove its interior. If $Q$ is the remaining ambient piece, excision gives $H_j(W,Q;R_n)=R_n$ only for $j=3$. The map $H_3(W;R_n)\to H_3(W,Q;R_n)$ is an isomorphism: the boundary fundamental class meets the spanning arc once. The pair sequence therefore makes $Q$ an $R_n$-homology ball. Glue the two such complements on $S^2\times I$, joining the annulus strips. Mayer–Vietoris gives $R_n$ in degrees0 and3 and zero in other positive degrees; the endpoint connected-sum spheres give the degree3 generator, so each end inclusion is a homology isomorphism. The resulting smooth annulus witnesses connected-sum compatibility in the original localized category. These calculations use no homeomorphism-to-product assertion.

Thus connected sum is well defined in every category: the retained standard smooth construction handles $\mathcal C_{\mathrm{sm}}$, [F5] handles TOP/exotic, and step2.2 handles the localized case. The oriented knot connected-sum monoid [F3] descends to each quotient, giving associativity, commutativity and the unknot identity. The ribbon inverse in [F2], admissible in all four ambients, supplies the stated reverse-mirror inverse. All ambient and coefficient conditions are those of [F1].

Let V=S¹×D² be the standard oriented solid torus, with oriented core, meridional disk and product longitude. A pattern is a smooth oriented knot P in the interior of V. Its winding number w(P) is its algebraic intersection with an oriented meridional disk, equivalently the coefficient of the core in [P]∈H₁(V;Z). For a smooth oriented knot K in S³, let e_K:V→S³ be a zero-framed tubular embedding carrying the core to K and carrying the meridian and product longitude to the positive meridian and preferred longitude of K. The satellite knot P(K) is e_K(P).

When concordance preservation has been established, the formula [K]↦[P(K)] defines a set map on each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n}. The solid-torus meridian is strong winding number ±1 for P if, after V is embedded as the standard unknotted solid torus and P(U) denotes the resulting closure, that meridian normally generates π₁(S³\P(U)). Normal generation means that the smallest normal subgroup containing the element is the whole group. Strong winding number ±1 is a separate condition from ordinary winding number ±1. No additivity or homomorphism property is part of this definition.

Let P be an oriented pattern of winding n≠0 and K an oriented knot. If P(U) bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B whose oriented boundary is identified with the standard oriented S³ and H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i, then for every K the zero surgeries M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly R_n-homology cobordant. For the positive meridians determined by the supplied orientations, their images in the cobordism satisfy [mu_K]=n[mu_{P(K)}]; in particular they differ by a unit of R_n. This is a winding-unit meridian comparison, not a claim of literal equality for arbitrary winding. If P has strong winding number ±1 and P(U) is pseudo-slice (respectively locally flat topologically slice), then M(P(K)) and M(K) are smoothly (respectively topologically) homology cobordant through a 4-manifold whose fundamental group is normally generated by the image of the fundamental group of either boundary component. The category and closure hypotheses are separate and cannot be inferred from winding alone.

Let knots be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented S³ and let I=[0,1]. Let C_sm be their smooth concordance classes, where equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in S³×I. Let C_top be their locally flat topological concordance classes in that product. Let C_ex be their exotic-smooth concordance classes: equivalence is witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W together with an orientation-preserving homeomorphism of pairs (W,∂W)≅(S³×I,S³×{0,1}) matching the endpoint knots. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, and it has product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. For a nonzero integer n set R_n=Z[1/|n|]. Let C^{1/n} be the classes under equivalence witnessed by a smooth proper annulus in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold W with boundary the two standard endpoint 3-spheres such that each boundary inclusion induces an isomorphism H_i(S³;R_n)→H_i(W;R_n) for every i. The annulus is oriented so that its boundary is −K₀ at the lower end and K₁ at the upper end, with product collars at both ends agreeing with the ambient boundary collars. A knot is pseudo-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold homeomorphic to B⁴, with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³. A knot is Z[1/|n|]-slice if it bounds a smooth proper disk in a compact smooth oriented 4-manifold B with its oriented boundary identified with the standard oriented S³ and with H_i(B;R_n)≅H_i(B⁴;R_n) for every i; such a B is an R_n-homology 4-ball. These are sets of equivalence classes; this definition alone asserts no group structure.

Assume AC_ω. Under connected sum, each of C_sm, C_top, C_ex and C^{1/n} is an abelian group. The identity is the class of the unknot, and the inverse of [K] is the class of the reverse mirror of K. Each category retains the ambient and coefficient conditions in its definition.

Let B be a smooth 4-ball embedded in the standard smooth 4-sphere S⁴. The closure of S⁴\B is diffeomorphic to the standard 4-ball. This is the special smooth Schoenflies complement assertion used after a capped contractible 4-manifold has been identified with standard S⁴; it does not assert the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture.

Let P be a pattern and let K be a knot. Choose a transverse meridional disk for P and a short product slab about it. Form a pattern P_K by replacing all strands of P across that slab by parallel untwisted copies of a long-knot representative of K, with the individual strand orientations inherited from P; this is simultaneous companion insertion, rather than tying K into just one arc. For every knot J, the satellite P(K#J) is isotopic as an oriented knot to P_K(J). The pattern P_K has the same winding number as P.

Let P⊂S¹×D² be a smooth oriented pattern. If oriented knots K₀ and K₁ are concordant in one of the four categories C_sm, C_top, C_ex or C^{1/n}, then P(K₀) and P(K₁) are concordant in the same category. Thus P induces a well-defined set map on each of these concordance sets.

Let A be a proper annulus in a compact oriented 4-manifold W, with boundary knots K₀ and K₁ in the two boundary 3-spheres. Assume A has an oriented normal disk neighborhood A×D² whose endpoint framings are the preferred zero-linking longitudes. Let R be Z or R_n=Z[1/|n|], and assume each end S³→W is an R-homology isomorphism. Removing A×D² and attaching D²×S¹×I along the annular side, with ∂D² matched to the annulus longitude and the core matched to the normal meridian, produces a cobordism V from M(K₀) to M(K₁). The statement predicts that the boundary inclusions M(K_i)→V are R-homology isomorphisms. If W is simply connected, it also predicts that π₁(V) is normally generated by either endpoint knot-group image.

Let P be a pattern of strong winding number ±1. For every oriented knot K, regard P(K) as the pattern obtained by tying K into each strand of P in the companion solid torus. Then this new pattern P(K) also has strong winding number ±1. A pattern obtained from any strong-winding pattern by taking connected sum with a local knot also has strong winding number ±1.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K\subset S^3$, let $B^4=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\lVert x\rVert^2\le1\}$ with boundary $S^3$. The oriented connected sum $K\#K^\dagger$ bounds a smooth properly embedded disk $D\subset B^4$ for which the squared radial function $\rho(x)=\lVert x\rVert^2$ restricts to a Morse function on the interior of $D$ with all critical points of index $0$ or $1$.

derivations.claim: Apply [F13] to the finite compact input for the branch at hand. For TOP the ambient product or ball is already standard; for the exotic branch its actual marked product/ball homeomorphism is given and is encoded in both directions. Use two coding passes. First encode only this finite compact geometry by a real $r_0$. In $L[r_0]$, before imposing any localized homology or strong-winding condition, use the ordinary finite smooth Morse construction to obtain finite handle/CW presentations of the supplied smooth ambient manifolds and finite presentations of the relevant knot exteriors, with their comparison maps, homotopies and peripheral markings. Export these purely geometric presentations and compact comparison certificates by [F13]. No choice-free generic-Morse theorem in $V$ is being assumed. Now work in $V$: its given localized homology hypothesis applies to these actual exported presentations. Over the PID $R_n$, the augmented finite free chain complex for an $R_n$-acyclic ball, or the mapping cone for either boundary inclusion, has a finite matrix contracting homotopy; finite row/column reduction supplies it. Likewise, the given strong-winding condition supplies, for each generator in the finite closure-knot presentation, an actual finite word expressing it as a product of conjugates of the designated axis meridian. There are only finitely many such generators and certificates, so choosing this list needs only finite choice. Enlarge $r_0$ to one real $r$ containing the presentations, their actual comparison certificates, these input group words and the finite contraction matrices. Their displayed equations $dh+hd=1$ and word identities are arithmetic, and establish the exact input homology and strong-winding hypotheses inside $L[r]$. No raw homology or fundamental-group absoluteness is asserted. In that model apply the unconditional CDR weak geometry, including [F11], [F12] and the finite connected-sum identities needed in [F4]. Export the resulting compact manifolds, disks, homeomorphisms and finite homology certificates using [F13]. Both stages carry finite normal-generation certificates: the input axis words just described accompany the final CDR call, and the output cobordisms are exported with explicit words expressing each generator in their finite presentations as a product of conjugates of the designated boundary generators. These are actual finite witnesses in $V$. The only ambient hypotheses in these applications are the actual coded ones, and no family of annuli or arbitrary points is selected. In the ordinary smooth branch export only the unconditionally constructed contractible smooth $B$ and its marked co-core; do not assume the ambient smooth Poincare hypothesis in $L[r]$. After decoding in $V$, cap the actual $B$ there, and only then use the supplied smooth Poincare hypothesis in step2.3.

Suppose P(K)=P(U), with the stated closure-slice hypothesis. By [F7] this equality is witnessed by a concordance annulus; the zero-surgery descent [F12], with the retained normal-GIVEN construction [F8], gives a meridian-preserving homology cobordism from M(P(K)) to M(P(U)). Applying [F2] to K and U gives cobordisms from M(P(K)) to M(K) and from M(P(U)) to M(U). On each pattern cobordism its marked first-homology relation is [mu_companion]=n[mu_satellite], where n is a unit in R_n; the concordance cobordism from [F8] identifies the two satellite meridian classes exactly. No equality of the pattern and companion preferred meridians is assumed.

Glue the cobordisms along the identified surgery manifolds. Mayer–Vietoris shows that the resulting boundary inclusions retain the required homology isomorphisms. In the exotic/topological branches, van Kampen shows the boundary normal-generation condition is preserved under this gluing. Hence M(K) and M(U) satisfy the corresponding surgery-cobordism relation. In the localized branch each endpoint meridian maps to a unit multiple of the same H_1 generator: compose the two winding-unit relations and the intervening exact concordance relation. In particular each endpoint meridian, including that of K, remains an R_n-module generator. In the strong-winding branches n=+1 or -1, so these multipliers are already integral units.

In the localized category, cap the M(U)=S¹×S² end with S¹×B³. Mayer–Vietoris gives an R_n-homology circle X with boundary M(K), and its meridian class is an R_n-module generator by step1.2. Attach a smooth 2-handle along that meridian with the surgery-dual zero framing. The relative pair (B,X) has only H_2(B,X;R_n)=R_n, generated by its core; its boundary map to H_1(X;R_n)=R_n is the meridian class, hence multiplication by a unit and an isomorphism. The pair sequence gives H_i(B;R_n)=0 for all i>0 and H_0(B;R_n)=R_n. The boundary handle description is the zero-surgery presentation for K together with its zero-framed meridian; this dual meridian surgery restores S³, and the 2-handle co-core has boundary K under that identification. Thus the resulting B is an R_n-homology ball containing the required smooth proper disk, proving K=U in C^{1/n}. Only a unit meridian multiplier was used, so the corrected [F2] supplies exactly the needed premise.

In the exotic and topological categories, the normal-generation condition makes the capped manifold after the meridian 2-handle contractible with boundary S³. The external input [F11] identifies this manifold with the boundary-marked topological $B^4$. Its co-core is smooth in the exotic branch and locally flat in the TOP branch, and its boundary is the original marked $K$. It therefore gives a pseudo-slice disk or a TOP slice disk respectively, proving $K=U$ in the required category.

In the ordinary smooth branch, work now in the ambient universe $V$: if P(U) is smoothly slice and P has strong winding ±1, the same cap and handle construction gives a contractible smooth 4-manifold B with boundary S³. Capping B with standard B⁴ gives a smooth homotopy S⁴; under the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture and [F5], B is diffeomorphic to B⁴.

Now suppose P(K)=P(J). By [F6], the connected-sum identity and the ribbon inverse give $P(J)=P_K(-K\#J)$ as concordance classes. Define R as the local connected sum of −P(K) with P_K. Then R(−K#J) is concordant to U because K#(−K#J) is concordant to J and satellites preserve concordance; moreover R(U)=−P(K)#P(K). By [F10], this closure is ribbon; [F6] gives w(R)=w(P).

If P has strong winding ±1, [F9] implies R also has strong winding ±1. The closure R(U) supplies the localized slice, pseudo-slice, topological-slice, and standard smooth-slice hypotheses in their respective branches. Apply the applicable earlier weak-injectivity branch to R to obtain $-K\#J=U$ and hence $K=J$.

Likewise, the given strong-winding condition supplies, for each generator in the finite closure-knot presentation, an actual finite word expressing it as a product of conjugates of the designated axis meridian. There are only finitely many such generators and certificates, so choosing this list needs only finite choice. Enlarge $r_0$ to one real $r$ containing the presentations, their actual comparison certificates, these input group words and the finite contraction matrices. Their displayed equations $dh+hd=1$ and word identities are arithmetic, and establish the exact input homology and strong-winding hypotheses inside $L[r]$. No raw homology or fundamental-group absoluteness is asserted. In that model apply the unconditional CDR weak geometry, including [F11], [F12] and the finite connected-sum identities needed in [F4]. Export the resulting compact manifolds, disks, homeomorphisms and finite homology certificates using [F13]. Both stages carry finite normal-generation certificates: the input axis words just described accompany the final CDR call, and the output cobordisms are exported with explicit words expressing each generator in their finite presentations as a product of conjugates of the designated boundary generators. These are actual finite witnesses in $V$. The only ambient hypotheses in these applications are the actual coded ones, and no family of annuli or arbitrary points is selected. In the ordinary smooth branch export only the unconditionally constructed contractible smooth $B$ and its marked co-core; do not assume the ambient smooth Poincare hypothesis in $L[r]$. After decoding in $V$, cap the actual $B$ there, and only then use the supplied smooth Poincare hypothesis in step2.3.

Now suppose P(K)=P(J). By [F6], the connected-sum identity and the ribbon inverse give $P(J)=P_K(-K\#J)$ as concordance classes. Define R as the local connected sum of −P(K) with P_K. Then R(−K#J) is concordant to U because K#(−K#J) is concordant to J and satellites preserve concordance; moreover R(U)=−P(K)#P(K). By [F10], this closure is ribbon; [F6] gives w(R)=w(P).

Suppose P(K)=P(U), with the stated closure-slice hypothesis. By [F7] this equality is witnessed by a concordance annulus; the zero-surgery descent [F12], with the retained normal-GIVEN construction [F8], gives a meridian-preserving homology cobordism from M(P(K)) to M(P(U)). Applying [F2] to K and U gives cobordisms from M(P(K)) to M(K) and from M(P(U)) to M(U). On each pattern cobordism its marked first-homology relation is [mu_companion]=n[mu_satellite], where n is a unit in R_n; the concordance cobordism from [F8] identifies the two satellite meridian classes exactly. No equality of the pattern and companion preferred meridians is assumed.

Glue the cobordisms along the identified surgery manifolds. Mayer–Vietoris shows that the resulting boundary inclusions retain the required homology isomorphisms. In the exotic/topological branches, van Kampen shows the boundary normal-generation condition is preserved under this gluing. Hence M(K) and M(U) satisfy the corresponding surgery-cobordism relation. In the localized branch each endpoint meridian maps to a unit multiple of the same H_1 generator: compose the two winding-unit relations and the intervening exact concordance relation. In particular each endpoint meridian, including that of K, remains an R_n-module generator. In the strong-winding branches n=+1 or -1, so these multipliers are already integral units.

In the localized category, cap the M(U)=S¹×S² end with S¹×B³. Mayer–Vietoris gives an R_n-homology circle X with boundary M(K), and its meridian class is an R_n-module generator by step1.2. Attach a smooth 2-handle along that meridian with the surgery-dual zero framing. The relative pair (B,X) has only H_2(B,X;R_n)=R_n, generated by its core; its boundary map to H_1(X;R_n)=R_n is the meridian class, hence multiplication by a unit and an isomorphism. The pair sequence gives H_i(B;R_n)=0 for all i>0 and H_0(B;R_n)=R_n. The boundary handle description is the zero-surgery presentation for K together with its zero-framed meridian; this dual meridian surgery restores S³, and the 2-handle co-core has boundary K under that identification. Thus the resulting B is an R_n-homology ball containing the required smooth proper disk, proving K=U in C^{1/n}. Only a unit meridian multiplier was used, so the corrected [F2] supplies exactly the needed premise.

In the exotic and topological categories, the normal-generation condition makes the capped manifold after the meridian 2-handle contractible with boundary S³. The external input [F11] identifies this manifold with the boundary-marked topological $B^4$. Its co-core is smooth in the exotic branch and locally flat in the TOP branch, and its boundary is the original marked $K$. It therefore gives a pseudo-slice disk or a TOP slice disk respectively, proving $K=U$ in the required category.

In the ordinary smooth branch, work now in the ambient universe $V$: if P(U) is smoothly slice and P has strong winding ±1, the same cap and handle construction gives a contractible smooth 4-manifold B with boundary S³. Capping B with standard B⁴ gives a smooth homotopy S⁴; under the smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture and [F5], B is diffeomorphic to B⁴.

If P has strong winding ±1, [F9] implies R also has strong winding ±1. The closure R(U) supplies the localized slice, pseudo-slice, topological-slice, and standard smooth-slice hypotheses in their respective branches. Apply the applicable earlier weak-injectivity branch to R to obtain $-K\#J=U$ and hence $K=J$.
