citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the oriented $S^3$ with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism and fix the standard height $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$. Its only critical points are the two poles, and each regular level is a 2-sphere. A **Morse representative** of a smooth oriented knot $K$ is a knot ambient isotopic to $K$ on which $h$ has only nondegenerate critical points. Define the **bridge number** $b(K)$ as the minimum number of local maxima of $h$ on a Morse representative of $K$. The standard unknot is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate 2-plane of $S^3$.

A **regular oriented diagram** is a projection of a smooth oriented knot with finitely many transverse double points, no other multiple points, and an over/under choice at each double point. A **crossing change** switches which branch is over at one chosen double point and leaves the projection and strand orientations unchanged. Define the **unknotting number** $u(K)$ as the minimum number of crossing changes needed to turn some regular diagram of a representative of $K$ into a diagram of the standard unknot. Both minima are taken in subsets of $\mathbb N$. The Morse-representative set is nonempty by the first well-definedness result below; under countable choice the regular-diagram existence result and the descending-diagram theorem below make the unknotting set nonempty. The bridge-number definition and the least-element argument in $\mathbb N$ require no choice; countable choice is used only to invoke the stated regular-projection supplier for $u(K)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. Let $A\subset M$ be a connected properly embedded incompressible annulus with $\partial A\subset\partial M$. If $A$ is boundary-compressible, then $A$ is boundary-parallel.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

For $n=2,3$, a given smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ into a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold is isotopic through embeddings to a small coordinate round ball, and that embedding isotopy extends ambiently with compact support. For a parametrized smooth $n$-ball $B$ and a parametrized smooth boundary $(n-1)$-disk $W$, the pair $(B,W)$ is diffeomorphic to the standard ball with a hemispherical window. The diffeomorphism can retain the specified window parameter, using stereographic parameters on the standard hemisphere and allowing the necessary orientation of that parameter. No choice axiom is assumed.

Consequently, attaching a parametrized smooth $n$-ball to a smooth $n$-manifold along such a window does not change its diffeomorphism type, provided an attaching collar and corner rounding are supplied. The resulting diffeomorphism is supported in the added ball and an arbitrarily small receiving collar. The inverse assertion holds for removing a ball that meets the boundary in exactly one such window with the supplied collar charts. In dimension two the windows are intervals.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.

derivations.claim: We first justify using bridge spheres for the height-based minimum in [F1]. In the product of regular height levels $S^2\times(-1,1)$, a maximum can be raised without changing the number or kinds of critical points: take a small cap containing only that maximum, perturb its horizontal location so that its central vertical ray misses the rest of the knot, narrow the cap inside its original small chart to fit a tube about that ray, and lift it along the ray, lengthening its two descending ends monotonically. The horizontal location is available arbitrarily close to the initial cap: the projection of the remaining finite collection of compact smooth arcs has empty interior, as follows by covering each arc by finitely many intervals of derivative bound $C$, whose projected images lie in disks of radius $C\delta$ and have total area tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. Compact disjointness then gives a narrow tube about the ray avoiding the rest of the knot; its two thin parallel sides are the lengthened ends. A horizontal cap perturbation and the subsequent vertical move have embedding tracks with no new extrema; the moving cap has the translated local quadratic maximum and the ends have strictly positive or negative height derivative. Extend with [F7]. Do this finitely many times, choosing distinct rays avoiding earlier cap tracks, until all maxima lie above a regular level above all minima. The upper and lower pieces are trivial tangles with simultaneous disjoint spanning disks: sweep their endpoints between successive critical heights, extending the finite point motions on each level sphere by disjoint small coordinate vector fields. Transport disjoint joining arcs by these level isotopies. At a cap choose its joining arc in its small cap chart, away from the finitely many earlier arcs (move those arcs off that chart by a level isotopy before the birth). Their swept traces, capped at the extrema, give pairwise disjoint disks. Conversely, for any smooth bridge sphere and displayed disks, [F6] first carries the sphere to a regular level. Push each bridge through its own disk to a thin collar of its foot; in disk parameters use a positive rounded arch whose height is $\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ above, and $-\varepsilon\sin(\pi t)$ below, with compatible endpoint collars. The disjoint same-side disks allow these isotopies simultaneously; [F7] extends them, and rounding at endpoints gives exactly one maximum per upper arc and one minimum per lower arc. Thus the minimum number of upper arcs over bridge spheres is exactly the height-defined $b$. In particular a minimum-height representative supplies a bridge sphere with $b$ upper arcs, and any factor bridge sphere with $n$ upper arcs gives $b(\text{factor})\le n$.
Choose bridge representatives realizing $b(K)$ and $b(J)$, which is possible by [F1] and step 1.1. Each comes with its bridge sphere and disjoint upper and lower bridge-spanning disks.

Choose one point of each knot on its bridge sphere where an upper bridge arc and a lower bridge arc meet. Take product-coordinate balls around the two points so each ball meets the sphere in a disk, the knot in one short arc crossing that disk once, and each of the two incident bridge-spanning disks in a half-disk. Remove the ball interiors and glue the punctured spheres by the connected-sum map from [F2]. The two selected upper bridge arcs join into one proper upper arc, and the two selected lower bridge arcs join into one proper lower arc. The new upper spanning disk is the union of the two punctured upper disks and the gluing rectangle; two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk. The same construction gives the lower spanning disk. Every unselected bridge arc and disk remains unchanged and disjoint from these disks. Thus the connected-sum position has $b(K)+b(J)-1$ upper arcs, so $b(K\#J)\le b(K)+b(J)-1$.

If either factor is the unknot, [F8] gives equality immediately. Suppose therefore both are nontrivial. Choose a bridge sphere $S$ of $L=K\#J$ with $b=b(L)$ upper arcs, by step 1.1. Transport the connected-sum construction's two-puncture sphere through the representative isotopy; this gives a smooth sphere $P$ cutting $L$ into the specified factors. Choose a sufficiently small product tube adapted to its two transverse punctures and form $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(L)$. The annulus core is a positive or negative meridian in the tube: both its boundary components bound the normal disks $P\cap N(L)$ and its core is homotopic within $A$ to either boundary. By [F4], composing $\pi_1(A)=\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(E_L)$ with abelianization sends its generator to $\pm1\in\mathbb Z$. The inclusion is therefore injective.

There is no boundary compression of $A$. If there were, [F5] would give a parallelism to one of the two annuli $A_0$ on the boundary torus between its meridional boundaries. This implies that one factor is the unknot, as can be checked with the markings: write the tube over the corresponding subinterval of the core knot as $D^2\times I$, with side $A_0=\partial D^2\times I$ and end disks the two disks $P\cap N(L)$. Attach the annulus parallelism to this side, retaining its rim collars. It merely enlarges the radial disk coordinate in each $I$-fiber, so the result is a ball with boundary the original $P$ after rounding. Its knot arc is the core $\{0\}\times I$, and it cobounds with an arc on that ball's boundary a disk given by a fixed radial interval times $I$, rounded at its ends. Capping this arc on $P$ produces an unknot. The same construction works for either complementary annulus of the torus; it uses its actual product parameter, not just a homological slope. By [F8] the resulting unknot is one of the given factors, contradicting nontriviality. Thus all hypotheses of [F3] hold for this particular $P$, and we may apply its isotopy and disk changes without changing $(L,S)$ or the specified factors.

In the resulting normal form $P\cap S=C$ is one circle disjoint from $L$. The two disks $P_\pm=P\cap B_\pm$ each contain one puncture. Indeed the two disk-intersection arcs of [F3] have their puncture endpoints one on each side, as in that lemma's final normalization. Each $P_\pm$ is a proper disk cutting its bridge ball into two balls: cap it by either of the two disks on $\partial B_\pm$ bounded by its rim, round, and apply [F6]; the side not containing the exterior of $B_\pm$ is the required ball. Its two endpoints on $S$ lie on opposite sides of $C$, because the bridge crosses that separating disk once. Every other bridge arc is wholly on one side. Consequently $r_i$ is odd.

Cap each of the two cut ball-arcs of $L$ by a boundary arc on $P$ running from the upper puncture to the lower puncture and crossing $C$ once, chosen as the two type-I traces joined by an arc of $C$ between their distinct foot endpoints, then rounded slightly in the collar of $C$ so that it crosses $C$ transversely just once. Push the two caps into their respective boundary collars. On each side this cap is a trivial ball-arc meeting the capped bridge sphere $S_i\cup$(cap disk) once. Its upper and lower portions extend the severed bridge arcs. Every uncut bridge disk remains in its original region. Each of the two cut bridge disks is cut along its one trace into two disks; on each side join its disk piece to the narrow cap strip. This is a disk attached along one boundary interval, so gives a spanning disk for the extended upper or lower arc. Choose the cap strips in disjoint small quadrant collars of the traces; other disks miss them, and on a given side all disk pieces were originally disjoint. Step 1.1 applied to the two factor bridge spheres gives $b(K)\le n_1$ and $b(J)\le n_2$. Hence $b(K)+b(J)-1\le n_1+n_2-1=b=b(K\#J)$. Together with step 3.1 and the unknot case in step 2.2, this proves the formula for every pair of smooth oriented knots in the Statement. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Identify the oriented $S^3$ with the unit sphere in $\mathbb R^4$ by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism and fix the standard height $h(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=x_4$. Its only critical points are the two poles, and each regular level is a 2-sphere. A **Morse representative** of a smooth oriented knot $K$ is a knot ambient isotopic to $K$ on which $h$ has only nondegenerate critical points. Define the **bridge number** $b(K)$ as the minimum number of local maxima of $h$ on a Morse representative of $K$. The standard unknot is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate 2-plane of $S^3$.

A **regular oriented diagram** is a projection of a smooth oriented knot with finitely many transverse double points, no other multiple points, and an over/under choice at each double point. A **crossing change** switches which branch is over at one chosen double point and leaves the projection and strand orientations unchanged. Define the **unknotting number** $u(K)$ as the minimum number of crossing changes needed to turn some regular diagram of a representative of $K$ into a diagram of the standard unknot. Both minima are taken in subsets of $\mathbb N$. The Morse-representative set is nonempty by the first well-definedness result below; under countable choice the regular-diagram existence result and the descending-diagram theorem below make the unknotting set nonempty. The bridge-number definition and the least-element argument in $\mathbb N$ require no choice; countable choice is used only to invoke the stated regular-projection supplier for $u(K)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For two smooth oriented knots, changing either representative by oriented ambient isotopy, changing the sufficiently small coordinate ball and trivial subarc used for either knot, or changing the positive local frame used to identify that ball with the standard oriented ball does not change the oriented ambient-isotopy class of the connected-sum knot, when the boundary gluing map is the fixed standard orientation-reversing map from the definition.

Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K=K_1\#K_2$ be a smooth oriented connected sum with both factors nontrivial. Let $S$ be a regular level sphere giving a bridge position: $S$ divides $S^3$ into two balls, and in each ball the knot is a finite collection of properly embedded arcs, each of which cobounds an embedded disk with an arc on $S$; the disks in each ball are pairwise disjoint. Let $P$ be a smooth decomposing sphere meeting $K$ transversely in two points and cutting it into the given two oriented factors. Put $E=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ and let $A=P\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$ be the resulting annulus, where $N(K)$ is a small closed tubular neighborhood. Assume the inclusion-induced map $\pi_1(A)\to\pi_1(E)$ is injective and that there is no embedded disk in $E$, with interior disjoint from $A\cup\partial E$, whose boundary is the union of a properly embedded arc in $A$ that does not cobound a disk in $A$ with a subarc of $\partial A$ and an arc in $\partial E$. Then, after isotoping $P$ through spheres meeting $K$ twice and changing only the bridge-spanning disk systems for the fixed pair $(K,S)$, one can arrange that $P\cap S$ is exactly one simple closed curve and that the union of the upper and lower bridge-spanning disks meets $P$ in exactly two arcs, each joining one point of $P\cap K$ to a point of $P\cap S$.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot with a chosen closed tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, and let $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Every smoothly embedded two-sphere in the interior of $E_K$ bounds a smoothly embedded closed three-ball contained in $E_K$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable irreducible $3$-manifold whose boundary components are tori. Let $A\subset M$ be a connected properly embedded incompressible annulus with $\partial A\subset\partial M$. If $A$ is boundary-compressible, then $A$ is boundary-parallel.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

For $n=2,3$, a given smooth ball embedding $e:D^n\to N$ into a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold is isotopic through embeddings to a small coordinate round ball, and that embedding isotopy extends ambiently with compact support. For a parametrized smooth $n$-ball $B$ and a parametrized smooth boundary $(n-1)$-disk $W$, the pair $(B,W)$ is diffeomorphic to the standard ball with a hemispherical window. The diffeomorphism can retain the specified window parameter, using stereographic parameters on the standard hemisphere and allowing the necessary orientation of that parameter. No choice axiom is assumed.

Consequently, attaching a parametrized smooth $n$-ball to a smooth $n$-manifold along such a window does not change its diffeomorphism type, provided an attaching collar and corner rounding are supplied. The resulting diffeomorphism is supported in the added ball and an arbitrarily small receiving collar. The inverse assertion holds for removing a ball that meets the boundary in exactly one such window with the supplied collar charts. In dimension two the windows are intervals.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Let $D\subset B^4$ be a smooth properly embedded disk with boundary knot
$K\subset S^3=\partial B^4$. Choose a product tubular neighborhood
$\nu(D)\cong D^2\times D^2$ whose intersection with $S^3$ is the chosen tube
$N(K)$, and let $X=\overline{B^4\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu(D)}$. Then the
inclusion $E_K\hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\cong}H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$$
carrying the positive meridian of $K$ to the positive normal-circle generator.

A smooth $f:M\to N$ is an immersion if $df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ is injective for every $p$, using the full tangent spaces. It is an embedding if it is an immersion and a homeomorphism onto its image. No neatness, properness, closed-image, or boundary-preservation condition is included.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

derivations.claim: Suppose $D\subset B_1$ is a smooth proper slice disk for $K$. Its oriented normal $2$-plane bundle is trivial because $D$ is a disk. Choose a nowhere-zero normal section and push $D$ slightly along it to a parallel disk $D'$ in the exterior $X$ of a tubular neighborhood of $D$. The boundary $K'$ is a degree-one parallel of $K$ in $E_K$, and it bounds $D'$ in $X$. By [F3], its class in $H_1(E_K)$ is zero. By [F2], it is the preferred longitude.

A tubular neighborhood of $D$ is $D^2\times D^2$ and meets the other hemisphere $B_2$ in the attaching region $S^1\times D^2$. Consequently $B_2\cup\nu(D)$ is obtained from a $4$-ball by attaching one $0$-framed $2$-handle along $K$, hence is diffeomorphic to $X_0(K)$ by [F1]. This union is a smooth codimension-zero submanifold of $S^4$.

Conversely, suppose $i:X_0(K)\hookrightarrow S^4$ is a smooth codimension-zero embedding. In the $0$-handle of $X_0(K)$ take the cone on $K$ from an interior point $p$, and join that cone disk to the core disk $D^2\times\{0\}$ of the $2$-handle along their common boundary $K$. After smoothing the join, this is a piecewise-smooth embedded $2$-sphere, smooth away from the cone point $p$.

In oriented coordinates at $p$ and $i(p)$, the derivative of $i$ is invertible by [F4], because its differential is injective and both dimensions are four. By [F5], $i$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$. If its local orientation sign is negative, compose it with a fixed orientation-reversing reflection of the standard $S^4$; this preserves the existence of the embedding and makes the local sign positive. Thus its derivative $A$ lies in $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$.

Identify the cone near $p$ with the radial cone on $K\subset S^3$. Along each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$, followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link $\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where $\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite $P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of $\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$. It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$.

Choose the coordinate ball bounded by that small sphere. Its complement $W=S^4\setminus\operatorname{int}(B_\epsilon)$ is a standard $4$-ball. The image sphere is smooth away from the cone point; transversality makes its remainder after deleting the cone cap a smooth properly embedded disk in $W$ with product boundary collar and boundary $\Gamma_\epsilon$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $C$ denote the Conway knot represented by the Conway diagram in Figure 1 of
Piccirillo's paper, and let $K_P$ denote the knot represented by the partner
diagram in Figure 2 of that paper. Choose an orientation on each diagram. The
symbols $C$ and $K_P$ refer to these specified diagram isotopy classes.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

Assume countable choice. Let $(B,G,R)$ be a dualizable framed handle link and
let $X(B,G,R)$ be its associated handlebody. There are finite sequences of
handle slides and cancellations, first sliding $G$ over $B$ and cancelling
the $1$-handle $R$ with the $2$-handle $B$, and then using the reversed roles,
that leave single $0$-framed attaching knots $K_G$ and $K_B$, respectively.
There are diffeomorphisms
$$
X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)\cong X_0(K_B).
$$

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $C$ denote the Conway knot represented by the Conway diagram in Figure 1 of
Piccirillo's paper, and let $K_P$ denote the knot represented by the partner
diagram in Figure 2 of that paper. Choose an orientation on each diagram. The
symbols $C$ and $K_P$ refer to these specified diagram isotopy classes.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

Assume countable choice. Let $(B,G,R)$ be a dualizable framed handle link and
let $X(B,G,R)$ be its associated handlebody. There are finite sequences of
handle slides and cancellations, first sliding $G$ over $B$ and cancelling
the $1$-handle $R$ with the $2$-handle $B$, and then using the reversed roles,
that leave single $0$-framed attaching knots $K_G$ and $K_B$, respectively.
There are diffeomorphisms
$$
X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)\cong X_0(K_B).
$$

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen closed product
tubular neighborhood $N(K)$, exterior $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$,
and positive meridian $\mu_K$. Then
$$H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_K].$$
The assertion uses integral singular homology and the stated tube convention.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a regular oriented diagram
of a two-component oriented link in $S^3$, with components $K_1,K_2$. Write
$$S(D):=\sum_{c\text{ between }K_1\text{ and }K_2}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
Then $S(D)$ is even, and
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(K_1,K_2):=\frac{S(D)}2\in\mathbb Z$$
is unchanged by planar isotopy and by each oriented Reidemeister move of types
I, II, and III. Thus it has the same value on any two regular diagrams of
ambient-isotopic oriented links. It is symmetric in $K_1,K_2$; reversing exactly
one component changes its sign, and reversing both components leaves it
unchanged.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude $\lambda_K$. Its smooth zero-trace $X_0(K)$ is the
compact smooth $4$-manifold obtained from $B^4$ by attaching a single $2$-handle
$D^2\times D^2$ to $\partial B^4=S^3$ along $K$, using the framing whose
parallel curve represents $\lambda_K$; corners are rounded.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $W$ be a compact smooth $n$-manifold with collared boundary $\partial W=\partial_0W\sqcup\partial_1W$, let $\varphi:S^{k-1}\times D^{n-k}\to\partial_1W$ be an attaching embedding of a $k$-handle and let $\psi:S^k\times D^{n-k-1}\to\partial_1(W\cup_\varphi h^k)$ be an attaching embedding of a $(k+1)$-handle attached after it, where $0\le k\le n-1$. If the attaching sphere of $h^{k+1}$ meets the belt sphere of $h^k$ transversely in exactly one point, then $W\cup_\varphi h^k\cup_\psi h^{k+1}$ is diffeomorphic to $W$ relative to $\partial_0W$. Consequently a geometrically cancelling consecutive pair may be deleted from, or added to, any handle presentation of the same manifold; the diffeomorphism may be taken to act only in a collar of the affected boundary disc and in the two handles, so the attaching data of all later handles are carried along.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen tubular neighborhood
and preferred longitude. Call $K$ smoothly slice when it bounds a smooth
properly embedded disk in the standard $B^4$, with a product collar at its
boundary. Then $K$ is smoothly slice if and only if the compact smooth
$4$-manifold $X_0(K)$, formed using that preferred-longitude framing, admits a
smooth codimension-zero embedding into the standard $S^4$.

derivations.claim: The standard spanning disk for $U$ in $B^4$ is a smooth proper slice disk. By [F4], its zero-trace embeds smoothly in $S^4$.

Glue the spanning disk for $U$ in the boundary $S^3$ to the core disk of the attached $2$-handle. Their union is an embedded $S^2$, and its regular neighborhood is the disk bundle over $S^2$ whose clutching map along the equator has degree equal to the handle framing. The framing is zero by [F1], so this clutching map has degree zero. Since $SO(2)\cong S^1$ and a degree-zero map $S^1\to S^1$ is null-homotopic, the oriented disk bundle is trivial. Therefore $X_0(U)\cong S^2\times D^2$.

The standard unknotted $S^2$ in $S^4$ has trivial oriented normal bundle: in the round model one normal vector is radial in $\mathbb R^3$ and the other is the constant fourth-coordinate vector. Its tubular neighborhood is thus $S^2\times D^2$, giving the stated embedding of $X_0(U)$.

Each of $B$ and $G$ bounds its chosen normal disk meeting the core $R$ once, so both indicated sublinks are a knot and its meridian. The disks are disjoint, so $B$ and $G$ have zero linking number. Their framings are zero by the stated preferred-longitude pushoffs. Thus $(B,G,R)$ satisfies [F2].

Cancel the $1$-handle represented by $R$ with the $2$-handle $B$ using their single transverse meridional intersection. The other normal disk is disjoint from this cancellation neighborhood; after cancellation it is a spanning disk for the remaining attaching circle. The transported framing is zero, so the remaining handle is $X_0(U)$. Reversing the roles gives the same result after cancelling $R$ with $G$. This verifies both cancellations described in the Example.
